nodeData.note: How to value the stock a business holds, using IAS 2: lower of cost and net realisable value, FIFO or weighted average, and how closing stock gives cost of sales.

children.topic: What inventory is and why it matters
children.note: Inventory (stock) is goods a business holds to sell or to use up making things. Getting its value right decides the profit figure and the current assets on the balance sheet.
The things on the shelves waiting to be sold: sugar and soap in a duka, medicines in a hospital pharmacy, spare parts in a garage.

manas.q: What is inventory?

children.note: Goods bought to resell; raw materials and parts waiting to be used in making; and work in progress or finished goods made by the business itself.
Closing inventory is taken away from purchases to get cost of sales. If it is wrong, gross profit and net profit are wrong by the same amount.
Closing inventory goes in two places: deducted in cost of sales in the income statement, and shown as a current asset in the statement of financial position.
Builds on final accounts of a sole trader (topic 6), where opening and closing inventory first appear, and on accruals (topic 7): we match the cost of goods sold to the sales they earned.
IAS 2 Inventories is the IFRS standard on how to value stock. Small Kenyan entities using IFRS for SMEs follow a section with almost the same rules.
Value inventory at whichever is lower: what it cost you, or what you can realistically get for it after selling costs. Never value it above cost.

manas.q: What is the basic valuation rule in IAS 2?

children.note: Net realisable value is the expected selling price less any costs to finish the item and costs needed to sell it.

manas.q: How is net realisable value (NRV) calculated?

children.note: It stops a business showing profit it has not yet earned. A loss you can already see (damaged or expiring stock) is recognised now.

children.topic: Item by item, not in total
children.note: Compare cost and NRV for each item (or group of similar items) separately. A gain on one product must not hide a loss on another.

manas.q: Is the cost vs NRV comparison done in total or item by item?

children.note: Common causes: damage, expiry dates near (medicines), goods going out of fashion, selling prices falling, or high costs still needed to sell.
The drop to NRV is an expense of the period, usually put in cost of sales: Dr Cost of sales / Cr Inventory.

manas.q: What is the double entry to write inventory down to NRV?

children.note: Many small Kenyan businesses report under IFRS for SMEs. Its inventory section also uses lower of cost and selling price less costs to complete and sell.
Cost is everything spent to get the goods to their present place and condition, ready to sell. Some costs must be left out.
Purchase price, import duty and non-refundable taxes, carriage inwards (transport to your store), handling, and for a maker, direct labour and production overheads.

manas.q: What costs are included in the cost of inventory?

children.note: Trade discounts, rebates and similar reductions lower the cost of the goods. Refundable VAT you can claim back from KRA is not part of cost.
Storage after the goods arrive (unless needed in production), selling and advertising costs, general admin overheads, and abnormal waste.

manas.q: Name costs excluded from inventory cost.

children.note: Carriage inwards (bringing goods in) is part of cost. Carriage outwards (delivering to customers) is a selling expense, never part of inventory.

manas.q: Is carriage outwards part of inventory cost?

children.note: A manufacturer adds a share of factory overheads (factory rent, machine depreciation) based on normal output, not on a slow or unusually busy month.
When identical items are bought at different prices, we need a rule for which cost goes out with each sale. IAS 2 allows FIFO or weighted average.
Used for unique, costly items like cars or land plots: each item keeps its own actual cost.
Assume the oldest stock is sold first. Closing inventory is valued at the most recent purchase prices.

manas.q: What does FIFO assume?

children.note: Each unit is valued at the average cost of all units available. Average = total cost of units ÷ number of units.

manas.q: How is weighted average cost calculated?

children.note: A new average is worked out after every purchase. Sales are costed at the average at that moment.
One average for the whole period: total cost of opening stock plus purchases ÷ total units. Simpler, but gives a slightly different answer.
Last in, first out is banned under IFRS and IFRS for SMEs. KASNEB may still ask about it, but your answer should say it is not permitted.

manas.q: Is LIFO allowed under IAS 2?

children.note: When prices rise, FIFO gives a higher closing stock and higher profit than AVCO, because the cheaper old stock is charged to cost of sales first.
Use the same method for inventories of a similar nature and use, and do not switch from year to year without a good reason.
A business can track stock all the time (perpetual) or only count it at the end (periodic).
Purchases go to a purchases account. Stock is counted at period end and cost of sales is worked out as a balancing figure. Common in small dukas.

manas.q: What is a periodic inventory system?

children.note: Every receipt and issue updates the stock record straight away, so stock and cost of sales are always known. Common with tills and pharmacy software.

manas.q: What is a perpetual inventory system?

children.note: The record for each item showing receipts, issues and balance in units and KES, under FIFO or AVCO.
Opening inventory + purchases (plus carriage in, less returns out) − closing inventory = cost of sales.

manas.q: What is the cost of sales formula?

children.note: In a periodic system at year end: Dr Inventory (balance sheet) / Cr Cost of sales (income statement) with the closing value. It becomes next year's opening stock.
Counting what is physically on the shelves. Even with perpetual records, a count is needed to find theft, breakage and recording errors.
Extra points that often turn up in exam questions on closing inventory.
If stock is counted a few days after the year end, adjust back to the year-end date using what happened in between.

manas.q: How do you adjust a stock count taken after the year end?

children.note: Goods sold after the year end were still on the shelves at the year end. Add back their cost (not selling price) to the count.
Goods received after the year end were not there at the year end. Deduct them from the count.
When the owner takes stock for personal use, at cost: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases. It is not a sale and is not a business expense.

manas.q: What is the entry for goods taken by the owner?

children.note: Goods sent to a customer on sale or return still belong to you until accepted. Include them in your inventory at cost.
Count it separately and write it down to NRV, which may be nil for expired medicines.
All figures checked: each answer adds up.
Hospital pharmacy, paracetamol boxes, January. Opening 100 @ KES 200. Buy 200 @ 230 on 5th. Sell 250 on 10th. Buy 150 @ 250 on 20th. Sell 120 on 28th. 80 boxes left.
80 boxes @ 250 = KES 20,000. Check: 83,500 + 20,000 = 103,500, the total cost of all goods available.
One average: 103,500 ÷ 450 boxes = 230. Closing 80 × 230 = 18,400; cost of sales 85,100.
Sales 250 @ 350 + 120 @ 380 = 133,100. Gross profit: FIFO 49,600; perpetual AVCO 49,000. Prices rose, so FIFO shows more profit.
Duka year: opening stock 120,000, purchases 850,000, carriage in 15,000, returns out 25,000, owner took goods 10,000, closing stock 140,000. Cost of sales = KES 810,000.
Sales 1,200,000 − cost of sales 810,000 = gross profit KES 390,000.
Dr Drawings 10,000 / Cr Purchases 10,000. Net purchases fall to 840,000 before carriage and returns.
Imported stock: price 500,000, trade discount 25,000, import duty 40,000, transport to store 15,000, storage later 8,000, advertising 12,000. Cost = 500,000 − 25,000 + 40,000 + 15,000 = KES 530,000.

children.topic: Why two costs are left out
children.note: Storage after arrival (8,000) and advertising (12,000) are expenses of the period, not part of the stock's cost.

children.topic: Example 4: lower of cost and NRV
children.note: Item A cost 40,000, NRV 55,000 → 40,000. Item B cost 30,000, sells for 22,000 less 2,000 costs, NRV 20,000 → 20,000. Item C cost and NRV 25,000 → 25,000. Value KES 85,000.
Total cost 95,000 − value 85,000 = 10,000. Dr Cost of sales 10,000 / Cr Inventory 10,000.
Total NRV is 100,000, above cost, but the loss on item B must still be recognised. Item by item gives 85,000.
Year end 31 Dec; count on 3 Jan at cost 260,000. Sales 1–3 Jan were 40,000 at selling price with 25% margin, so cost 30,000. Goods received 1–3 Jan 18,000.
Watch for these; they cost marks.
Stock is valued at cost (or NRV if lower), never at selling price. Remove the profit element first.
Margin is profit as a % of selling price; mark-up is profit as a % of cost. 25% margin means cost is 75% of sales; 20% mark-up means cost = sales ÷ 1.2.

manas.q: What is the difference between margin and mark-up?

children.note: LIFO is not permitted under IFRS. If asked, explain it and state that it cannot be used.
Carriage outwards, advertising and shop staff wages are not inventory cost.
If closing stock is overstated by 10,000, this year's profit is overstated by 10,000 and next year's profit is understated by 10,000.

manas.q: What is the effect of overstating closing inventory?

children.note: Goods taken by the owner are recorded at cost to drawings, not as sales.
Try each one, then open the bubbles for the steps.
Cost 12,000. Can sell for 15,000 after a repair costing 4,000. What value goes in the accounts?
Lower of cost 12,000 and NRV 11,000 = KES 11,000; write down 1,000.
Opening 50 units @ 100. Buy 100 @ 130. Sell 120. Find closing stock and cost of sales under FIFO and AVCO.
Year end 30 June; count on 5 July 480,000 at cost. Sales 1–5 July 60,000 at 20% mark-up. Goods received 22,000. Customer returns 6,000 at selling price.

children.topic: Step 1: cost of sales and returns
children.note: Sales at cost 60,000 ÷ 1.2 = 50,000 (add back). Returns at cost 6,000 ÷ 1.2 = 5,000 (deduct: they came back after the year end).

nodeData.note: Many small businesses keep only a cash book, receipts and M-Pesa statements, not full double entry. This topic shows how to rebuild the missing figures and still produce a profit figure and final accounts.

children.note: Records are incomplete when the owner has not kept a full set of double-entry books. The accountant has to fill the gaps from whatever evidence exists.
A business has incomplete records when some books or figures are missing, so a trial balance cannot be drawn up straight from the ledger.

manas.q: What are incomplete records?

children.note: Single entry means each transaction is written down once, usually in a cash book, with no matching second entry. It is simple but does not prove itself the way double entry does.

manas.q: What is single-entry bookkeeping?

children.topic: Typical duka: cash book and M-Pesa
children.note: A duka owner may have a notebook of cash takings, M-Pesa and bank statements, supplier invoices and a stock count. That is often all the accountant gets.
Common reasons: no time or skill for bookkeeping, records lost in fire, flood or theft, or a cashier who stole and destroyed papers.
The owner still needs a profit figure for KRA tax returns, a bank or SACCO loan, and to know if the business is doing well. KASNEB exams test this every few sittings.
Method 1: compare net assets at the start and end of the year (statement of affairs). Method 2: rebuild the accounts to find sales and purchases, then prepare a full income statement.

manas.q: What are the two main approaches to incomplete records?

children.note: A statement of affairs is a list of what the business owns and owes on one date. Comparing two of them shows how much the owner’s stake grew.
A list of assets and liabilities on a given date, made from counts, statements and estimates instead of a ledger. Assets minus liabilities gives the owner’s capital.

manas.q: What is a statement of affairs?

children.note: From topic 2, the accounting equation: assets minus liabilities equals capital. So if we can count net assets, we know the capital.

manas.q: Why do net assets equal capital?

children.note: Opening capital is the net assets at the start of the year: total opening assets less opening liabilities. Exams often hide it and expect you to work it out.

manas.q: How do you find opening capital when it is not given?

children.note: Profit = closing net assets − opening net assets + drawings − capital introduced. A negative answer is a loss.

manas.q: What is the formula for profit from change in net assets?

children.note: Money the owner took out reduced net assets but was not a business loss. Adding it back shows what the business really earned.

manas.q: Why are drawings added back when finding profit from net assets?

children.note: New money the owner put in raised net assets without being earned by trading. Taking it off removes that boost.

manas.q: Why is capital introduced deducted when finding profit from net assets?

children.note: It gives only one profit figure, not sales, cost of sales or expenses. It also cannot show errors or theft, so a full reconstruction is better when evidence allows.
When you have more evidence, rebuild T-accounts and let the missing figure be the balancing number. This is the heart of the topic.
Put every known figure into a T-account. The one missing amount is whatever makes both sides equal.

manas.q: What is the balancing-figure (missing figure) technique?

children.note: Rebuild cash and bank/M-Pesa from opening balance, receipts, payments and closing balance. The balancing figure is often drawings, cash sales or stolen cash.

manas.q: Which figures are usually found as the balancing figure in the cash account?

children.note: Credit sales = closing receivables + cash received from customers + discounts allowed + bad debts written off − opening receivables. This is the receivables control account from topic 12.

manas.q: How do you find credit sales from a receivables account?

children.note: Credit purchases = closing payables + cash paid to suppliers + discounts received − opening payables.

manas.q: How do you find credit purchases from a payables account?

children.note: Add cash sales (from the cash book or M-Pesa till) to credit sales from the receivables account to get total sales.
Expense for the year = cash paid − opening accrual + closing accrual. Topic 7 rules still apply.

manas.q: How do you find an expense when there are opening and closing accruals?

children.note: Expense for the year = cash paid + opening prepayment − closing prepayment.
Use last year’s carrying amount, add assets bought (from the cash book), take off disposals and depreciation (topic 8).
Some owners pay suppliers or themselves from the till before banking. Add those payments back to banked takings to find the true takings.
Gross profit can be expressed against cost (mark-up) or against selling price (margin). Exams use them to find a missing sales or cost of sales figure.
Mark-up is gross profit as a percentage of cost of sales. A 25% mark-up on a KES 800 item adds KES 200, so it sells for KES 1,000.

manas.q: What is mark-up?

children.note: Margin is gross profit as a percentage of sales. The same KES 200 profit on a KES 1,000 sale is a 20% margin.

manas.q: What is gross margin?

children.note: Mark-up 25%: cost 100, profit 25, sales 125. Margin 20%: sales 100, profit 20, cost 80. Write the table first, then scale it.

manas.q: How do you set up a cost structure for mark-up and margin?

children.note: Margin = mark-up ÷ (1 + mark-up). 25% mark-up = 0.25 ÷ 1.25 = 20% margin.

manas.q: How do you convert a mark-up into a margin?

children.note: Mark-up = margin ÷ (1 − margin). 20% margin = 0.20 ÷ 0.80 = 25% mark-up.

manas.q: How do you convert a margin into a mark-up?

children.note: Sales = cost of sales × (1 + mark-up). Cost of sales KES 240,000 at 25% mark-up gives sales of KES 300,000.

children.topic: Finding cost of sales from sales
children.note: Cost of sales = sales × (1 − margin). Sales KES 300,000 at 20% margin gives cost of sales of KES 240,000.

children.topic: Inventory lost by fire or theft
children.note: If stock is burnt or stolen, the count is gone. You estimate what should have been there using the usual margin.
Expected inventory = opening inventory + purchases − cost of sales, where cost of sales comes from sales and the normal margin or mark-up.

manas.q: How do you estimate inventory lost in a fire or theft?

children.note: Take off any stock that was saved or recovered. What is left is the loss to claim from the insurer or write off.
Dr Insurance claim receivable (amount agreed); Dr Income statement for any uninsured part; Cr Purchases (or cost of sales) with the full loss.

manas.q: What entries record inventory lost when part is covered by insurance?

children.note: An uninsured theft is an expense in the income statement. If the owner took the goods, it is drawings instead: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases.
IAS 2 Inventories says inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value. The fire estimate is based on cost, matching topic 13.
One year, 1 Jan to 31 Dec, using a cash book, M-Pesa statements and stock counts. All figures in KES and checked to agree.
Fittings 40,000 + inventory 60,000 + receivables 15,000 + cash/M-Pesa 25,000 = 140,000, less payables 20,000. Opening capital = 120,000.
Fittings 36,000 + inventory 75,000 + receivables 18,000 + cash/M-Pesa 41,000 = 170,000, less payables 22,000. Closing net assets = 148,000.
She took 60,000 drawings and put in 20,000 of savings. Profit = 148,000 − 120,000 + 60,000 − 20,000 = 68,000.
Received from customers 210,000, discounts allowed 2,000, bad debt 1,000. Credit sales = 18,000 + 210,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 − 15,000 = 216,000. Add cash sales 84,000: total sales 300,000.
Paid suppliers 190,000 and got 3,000 discounts. Purchases = 22,000 + 190,000 + 3,000 − 20,000 = 195,000.
In: opening 25,000 + cash sales 84,000 + customers 210,000 + capital 20,000 = 339,000. Out: suppliers 190,000 + expenses 48,000 + closing 41,000 = 279,000. Drawings = 60,000.
120,000 − expenses 48,000 − depreciation 4,000 − bad debt 1,000 − discounts allowed 2,000 + discounts received 3,000 = 68,000. Same as the net assets method.
Short examples for each technique, with checked numbers in KES.
Cost of sales is 240,000 and the owner adds 25% to cost. Sales = 240,000 × 1.25 = 300,000; gross profit 60,000, which is a 20% margin.
Opening stock 50,000, purchases 200,000, sales 240,000 at 20% margin. Cost of sales 192,000, so expected stock 58,000. Stock saved 8,000: loss 50,000.
Insurer agrees to pay 40,000 of the 50,000. Dr Insurance claim 40,000; Dr Income statement (loss) 10,000; Cr Purchases 50,000.
Paid KPLC 30,000 in the year; owed 3,000 at the start and 5,000 at the end. Expense = 30,000 − 3,000 + 5,000 = 32,000.
Paid 66,000 rent; 6,000 prepaid at the start, 12,000 prepaid at the end. Expense = 66,000 + 6,000 − 12,000 = 60,000.
Most lost marks come from mixing up margin and mark-up or putting items on the wrong side of a T-account.
Mark-up is on cost, margin is on sales. Using 25% of sales when the question says 25% mark-up gives the wrong cost of sales.

manas.q: What is the most common trap with mark-up and margin?

children.note: Goods the owner took for home use are drawings too. Add them to drawings and remove them from purchases.
Discounts and bad debts reduce receivables without cash. Leave them out and credit sales come out too low.

children.topic: Using cash paid as the expense
children.note: Cash paid is not the expense when there are accruals or prepayments. Always adjust for opening and closing balances.
If opening capital is not given, build an opening statement of affairs first. Do not guess or leave it blank.
Payments made straight from takings never reach the bank statement. Add them back or sales will be understated.
Drawings are added, capital introduced is deducted. Swapping them is a classic error.
Try each question, then open the bubble to see the steps.
Net assets: 200,000 at the start, 260,000 at the end. Drawings 90,000; capital introduced 30,000. Find the profit.
60,000 + drawings 90,000 − capital introduced 30,000 = profit KES 120,000.

children.topic: Q2: Sales from cost of sales
children.note: Cost of sales is 450,000 and the gross margin is 25%. Find sales and the mark-up.
Gross profit 150,000 ÷ cost 450,000 = 33.3% mark-up.
Receivables 40,000 at the start, 55,000 at the end. Cash received 380,000; discounts allowed 5,000. Find credit sales.
Opening 40,000 + credit sales (missing).
Opening stock 80,000, purchases 320,000, sales 400,000 at a 25% mark-up. Stock saved 12,000. Find the loss.

nodeData.note: A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share the profits. This map shows how to keep each partner's money separate, share the profit fairly, and handle a partner joining, leaving or the business closing.

children.note: Two to many people run one business together to make a profit. Think of two pharmacists running a chemist in Kisumu, or friends sharing a matatu business.
A business carried on by two or more people together, aiming for profit. Each owner is called a partner.

manas.q: What is a partnership?

children.note: More money (capital) to start, shared skills, shared work and shared risk. It is also easy and cheap to set up compared with a company.
In an ordinary partnership each partner can be made to pay ALL the firm's debts from their own pocket if the business cannot. That is the big risk.

manas.q: What does unlimited liability mean for a partner?

children.note: Kenya has a Limited Liability Partnerships Act (2011). In an LLP a partner's risk is limited, but the firm must be registered. Check the law for current details.

children.topic: How it differs from a sole trader
children.note: The accounts look like a sole trader's, but the capital section is split per partner and the profit must be shared. That sharing is what this topic is about.
The partners' written deal on money matters. If there is no agreement on a point, the law fills the gap.
A written contract between partners saying how much each puts in, how profit is shared, salaries, interest and what happens if someone leaves.

manas.q: What does a partnership agreement usually cover?

children.note: Capital each partner brings, profit-sharing ratio, partner salaries, interest on capital, interest on drawings, limits on drawings, and rules for joining, leaving and closing.
Kenya's Partnerships Act (2012) sets the rules for partnerships. Its default rules apply only where the partners have NOT agreed something different.

children.topic: Default rules when nothing is agreed
children.note: If the agreement is silent, the usual default rules are the five in the next bubbles. Exam questions say "there is no partnership agreement" to test these.
With no agreement, profit and loss are split equally, no matter how much capital each put in.

manas.q: With no agreement, how are profits shared?

children.note: Partners get no interest on the capital they put in unless they agreed it.

manas.q: With no agreement, do partners get interest on capital?

children.note: No partner is paid a salary for working in the business, even if one works harder.
Partners are not charged interest on money they take out.

children.topic: Interest on a loan to the firm
children.note: A partner who lends the firm extra money (beyond capital) earns interest on it, even with no agreement, at a rate set by the Partnerships Act. Exam questions usually state the rate; check the current Act for the default.

manas.q: With no agreement, does a partner loan earn interest?

children.note: Each partner has their own accounts so we can see what the firm owes each one.
Shows the long-term money a partner put into the business. Under fixed capitals it changes only when a partner adds or withdraws capital for good.

manas.q: What is a partner's capital account?

children.note: Shows the partner's day-to-day share: salary, interest and profit share come in (credit); drawings and interest on drawings go out (debit).

manas.q: What goes into a partner's current account?

children.note: Fixed: capital stays the same and everything else goes through the current account. Fluctuating: no current account, so all items go straight to capital.

manas.q: What is the difference between fixed and fluctuating capitals?

children.note: If a partner took out more than they earned, the current account has a debit balance. It is shown as a minus in the capital section (or as a receivable from the partner).
Cash or goods a partner takes for personal use. Dr Drawings (or current account) / Cr Bank or Purchases. Drawings are NOT an expense of the business.

manas.q: Are partners' drawings an expense?

children.note: Money lent by a partner over and above capital. It is a liability of the firm, and its interest is an expense charged before net profit.

manas.q: Where does interest on a partner's loan go?

children.note: After net profit is found (as for a sole trader), the appropriation account shows how it is divided among the partners.
A statement below the income statement that splits net profit between partners: salaries, interest on capital and the rest in the profit-sharing ratio.

manas.q: What is the appropriation account?

children.note: Start with net profit, add interest on drawings, take off salaries and interest on capital, then share what is left (residual profit) in the agreed ratio.

manas.q: What is the order of items in the appropriation account?

children.note: A reward for work agreed between partners. It is a share of profit, NOT a wages expense, so it goes in the appropriation account.

manas.q: Is a partner's salary an expense?

children.note: A reward for the money each partner put in, e.g. 10% of capital. It goes in the appropriation account and is credited to each partner.

manas.q: How is interest on capital calculated?

children.note: A charge on partners who take money out early, to be fair to those who leave money in. It ADDS to profit available for sharing.

manas.q: Why does interest on drawings increase the profit to share?

children.note: The agreed split of what is left, e.g. 3:2 means one partner gets 3/5 and the other 2/5.

manas.q: What does a 3:2 profit-sharing ratio mean?

children.note: Salaries and interest are still credited if agreed. This makes the residual loss bigger, and that loss is shared in the PSR (debited to partners).
When a partner joins, retires or dies, the old firm ends and a new one starts. We must settle what each old partner has earned up to that day.
The extra value of a business above its net assets: loyal customers, good name, location. A joining partner should pay for a share of it.

manas.q: What is goodwill in a partnership?

children.note: Common exam methods: a number of years' average profit, or super profit (profit above a normal return) times a number of years. The question will tell you which.

manas.q: Name two ways to value goodwill.

children.topic: Goodwill not kept in the books
children.note: Most questions: credit old partners in OLD ratio, then debit all partners in NEW ratio, so no goodwill account is left. The net effect is fair to each partner.

manas.q: How is goodwill handled if it is not to remain in the books?

children.note: Before a change, assets and liabilities are restated to fair value. Gains go to Cr, losses to Dr; the net profit or loss is shared among OLD partners in the OLD ratio.

manas.q: Who shares a revaluation profit or loss?

children.note: A new partner brings capital (Dr Bank / Cr new capital). Then adjust for goodwill and revaluation so old partners keep what they built up.
Value goodwill and revalue assets, then add up the leaver's capital, current account and shares. Pay in cash or move the amount to a loan account.

manas.q: What is a retiring partner owed?

children.note: Same steps as retirement, plus a share of profit up to the date of death. The amount is owed to the dead partner's estate (executors).
After a change the partners agree a new ratio. Always check whether a question uses the old or the new ratio for each step.
When the partnership ends, assets are sold, debts are paid, and partners take whatever cash is left.
The ending of a partnership, for example by agreement, death, bankruptcy or a court order.

manas.q: What is dissolution of a partnership?

children.note: The account that collects the book value of assets sold and what they fetched. The difference is the profit or loss on closing, shared in PSR.

manas.q: What is the purpose of the realisation account?

children.note: 1 Move assets (not cash) to realisation. 2 Record sales and assets taken by partners. 3 Pay liabilities and costs. 4 Share profit/loss. 5 Pay partners from bank.
Dr that partner's capital / Cr Realisation at the agreed value. It is like the partner buying the asset.
Outside creditors first, then partner loans, then partners' capital. Bank and capital accounts must all end at zero.

manas.q: In what order is cash paid out on dissolution?

children.note: If a partner owes the firm, they pay in cash. If they cannot, an old English case (Garner v Murray) says the others bear the loss in ratio of last agreed capitals, unless agreed otherwise.
All figures in KES. Each one balances; check it yourself.
Wanjiku and Otieno run a pharmacy. Capitals: W 600,000, O 400,000. Net profit 500,000. Interest on capital 10%, O salary 120,000, PSR 3:2.
Interest on drawings W 8,000, O 5,000 = 13,000. Profit to share 500,000 + 13,000 = 513,000.
Less O salary 120,000 leaves 393,000. Less interest on capital W 60,000 + O 40,000 = 100,000 leaves 293,000.
Opening credit 20,000. Credits: salary 120,000 + interest 40,000 + profit 117,200 → total 297,200. Debits: drawings 180,000 + interest on drawings 5,000 = 185,000. Closing credit 112,200.
Two partners, no agreement, capitals 800,000 and 200,000, profit 300,000. Act defaults apply: no interest or salary, split equally: 150,000 each.
A partner draws 60,000 evenly over the year; rate 10%. On average money was out for 6 months: 60,000 × 10% × 6/12 = 3,000.
Kamau and Achieng share equally, capitals 500,000 each. Njeri joins for 1/4, bringing 300,000 cash. Goodwill 200,000, not kept. New ratio 3:3:2.
Dr Goodwill 200,000 / Cr Kamau capital 100,000, Cr Achieng capital 100,000.

children.topic: Write it off in new ratio
children.note: Dr Kamau 75,000, Dr Achieng 75,000, Dr Njeri 50,000 / Cr Goodwill 200,000. Goodwill account is now zero.
Before Njeri joins: building up 150,000, inventory down 30,000, allowance for receivables up 10,000.
Cr Revaluation 150,000 (building). Dr Revaluation 30,000 (inventory) and 10,000 (allowance). Net gain 150,000 − 40,000 = 110,000.
Dr Revaluation 110,000 / Cr Kamau 55,000, Cr Achieng 55,000 (old ratio 1:1). Both sides of the account now total 150,000.
Ali, Baraka, Chebet share 2:2:1; Chebet retires. Capital C 200,000, current account Cr 20,000. Goodwill 150,000, not kept. Ali and Baraka then share 1:1.
Dr Chebet capital 230,000, Dr Chebet current 20,000 / Cr Bank 100,000, Cr Chebet loan 150,000. Both sides 250,000.

children.topic: Example 8: dissolution of a matatu firm
children.note: Mutua and Wafula share 1:1. Matatu 1,200,000, spares 50,000, receivables 80,000, bank 70,000. Payables 100,000; capitals M 700,000, W 600,000.
Matatu sold 1,000,000; Mutua takes spares at 40,000; receivables pay 75,000; payables settled for 95,000; closing costs 20,000.
Most lost marks come from putting items in the wrong place or using the wrong ratio.

children.topic: Salary put in the income statement
children.note: Partner salaries and interest on capital are shares of profit. They go in the appropriation account, never as expenses.
Interest on a partner's LOAN is a true expense. Charge it before net profit, not in the appropriation account.
Interest on drawings is ADDED in the appropriation account and DEBITED to the partner's current account.
Goodwill created and revaluation shared: OLD ratio. Goodwill written off: NEW ratio. Realisation loss: the ratio in force at closing.
If the question says no agreement, apply the Act: equal shares, no salaries, no interest on capital, even if capitals differ.
On dissolution the bank and every capital account must close at nil. If not, recheck the realisation account.
Try each one, then open the bubbles below it for the steps.
A and B share 2:1. Interest on capital A 30,000, B 20,000. B salary 40,000. Show each partner's total.
A partner draws KES 48,000 evenly through the year. Rate 12% a year. Find the interest.
Average time out is 6 months: 48,000 × 12% × 6/12 = 2,880. Dr partner current / Cr appropriation.
X and Y share 3:2. Z joins; new ratio X:Y:Z 2:2:1. Goodwill 100,000, not kept.
X +20,000, Y nil, Z −20,000. Only X gave up share (3/5 to 2/5), so only X gains.
Assets with book value 500,000 sold for 560,000; closing costs 10,000; partners share equally.
Profit 560,000 − 500,000 − 10,000 = 50,000. Cr each partner's capital 25,000.

nodeData.note: How clubs, societies, churches and welfare groups keep and present accounts: receipts and payments, income and expenditure, and the accumulated fund.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Some groups exist to serve members or a cause, not to make money for owners. Their accounts show members how money was used.
A club, society, church, temple or welfare group run for its members or a cause. Any extra money goes back into the cause, not to owners.

manas.q: What is a not-for-profit organisation?

children.note: A golf or sports club, a residents' association, a church or temple, a school PTA, an old boys' society, a chama's welfare kitty.
There is no owner putting in capital. Instead, the members' share of net assets is called the accumulated fund.
Income above spending is a surplus; spending above income is a deficit. The words change, the logic of accruals stays the same.

manas.q: What do not-for-profit bodies call profit and loss?

children.note: Members at the annual general meeting (AGM), the committee, donors and the Registrar of Societies. They want to know: was our money used well?
Often a volunteer treasurer with a simple cash book. That is why exam questions start from cash records, like incomplete records.
It uses accruals and prepayments, depreciation, incomplete records and the trading account. Only the names and layout are new.
Each business word has a club word. Learn these pairs and the topic gets easy.
The club's own net worth: what it owns minus what it owes. It plays the role of capital in a sole trader.

manas.q: What is the accumulated fund?

children.note: Income for the year is more than expenditure. It is added to the accumulated fund.

manas.q: What is a surplus?

children.note: Expenditure for the year is more than income. It is taken off the accumulated fund.

manas.q: What is a deficit?

children.note: Yearly fees members pay to belong. They are the main income of most clubs.

manas.q: What are subscriptions?

children.note: Fees for this year that members still owe at year end. They are money owed to the club, so a current asset.

manas.q: How are subscriptions in arrears shown in the statement of financial position?

children.note: Fees members paid early for next year. The club owes them a year of membership, so a current liability.

manas.q: How are subscriptions in advance shown in the statement of financial position?

children.note: A one-off fee that lets a member belong for life. It is spread over several years, not all treated as income at once.
A joining fee paid once by new members. The club's rules decide if it is income or added to the fund.
Money given for one purpose only, like a church building fund. It is kept apart from general income.

manas.q: What is a special or restricted fund?

children.note: A club usually prepares four things: receipts and payments, a bar trading account, income and expenditure, and a statement of financial position.
A summary of the cash book: opening cash, plus all money in, minus all money out, gives closing cash.
Every cash and bank item, whatever year it relates to, capital or revenue. Arrears collected and new equipment both appear.

manas.q: What does a receipts and payments account include?

children.note: Non-cash items: depreciation, amounts owed, amounts unpaid, and inventory. So it does not show the true result for the year.
Debit side: opening balance and receipts. Credit side: payments and closing balance (the balancing figure).
The club's version of the income statement. It uses the accruals basis: only income earned and costs used up this year.
Revenue items for this year only: subscriptions due, bar profit, entrance fees (if income), rent, wages, depreciation.

manas.q: What is an income and expenditure account?

children.note: Capital items like buying equipment, and amounts belonging to other years such as arrears from last year.
Income minus expenditure gives the surplus or deficit for the year.
R&P is cash basis and a real account (it has a balance carried forward). I&E is accruals basis and a nominal account, closed off each year.

manas.q: Give two differences between R&P and I&E accounts.

children.note: Any trading activity gets its own small trading account. Bar takings less cost of drinks sold gives bar gross profit.
Sales less (opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory) = gross profit. Less bar wages = bar profit.

manas.q: What is the format of a bar trading account?

children.note: Purchases = cash paid to bar suppliers + closing bar payables − opening bar payables. Same as incomplete records.
Only the bar profit (or loss) moves to the I&E account as one line, not the whole bar sales figure.
Same as for a business, but the bottom part shows accumulated fund plus surplus instead of capital plus profit.

manas.q: What replaces capital in a club's statement of financial position?

children.note: If not given, work it out: opening assets minus opening liabilities. This is a statement of affairs, as in incomplete records.

manas.q: How do you find the opening accumulated fund?

children.note: These items cause most exam marks to be lost. Treat each one carefully.
A T-account that sorts cash received into last year, this year and next year. The balancing figure is this year's income.
Opening arrears (b/d), closing advance (c/d), and the I&E transfer, which is the balancing figure.
Opening advance (b/d), cash received in the year, and closing arrears (c/d).

manas.q: What goes on the credit side of a subscriptions account?

children.note: Income = cash received − opening arrears + closing arrears + opening advance − closing advance.

manas.q: What is the quick formula for subscriptions income?

children.note: If the club writes off old arrears, treat them like bad debts. Many clubs only count subscriptions when received; follow the question.
Credit the cash to a life membership fund. Each year move a fair share to I&E as income.
Dr Bank KES 200,000 / Cr Life membership fund KES 200,000. Ten members paid KES 20,000 each.
Spread over 10 years: Dr Life membership fund KES 20,000 / Cr I&E KES 20,000. Balance left: KES 180,000.

manas.q: How is a life membership fee treated each year?

children.note: The unused balance sits below the accumulated fund in the statement of financial position, as deferred income.
Check the club's policy. Either credit them to I&E as income, or add them straight to the accumulated fund.
Dr Bank KES 30,000 / Cr I&E (entrance fees) KES 30,000. The most common exam treatment unless told otherwise.
Dr Bank KES 30,000 / Cr Accumulated fund KES 30,000. Used when the rules say joining fees build the club.
General gifts are income in I&E. Gifts for a stated purpose go to a special fund.
A well-wisher gives a temple KES 50,000 with no conditions. Dr Bank 50,000 / Cr I&E (donations) 50,000.
A church harambee raises KES 500,000 for a new hall. Dr Bank 500,000 / Cr Building fund 500,000.
When the hall is built, the asset is recorded and the fund shows what was spent. Do not count it as general surplus.
Treat rent, electricity and wages exactly as in the accruals and prepayments topic. Adjust cash paid to find this year's cost.
Clubs depreciate equipment, furniture and buildings like any business. It is an expense in I&E, never in R&P.
Cash from the sale is a receipt in R&P. Only the profit or loss on disposal goes to I&E.
Year ended 31 Dec 2025. We go from cash records to full final accounts. Every figure ties back.
Bank 120,000; bar inventory 40,000; subs in arrears 15,000; equipment 300,000. Owed: subs in advance 6,000; bar payables 18,000.
Receipts 620,000: subs 210,000, bar takings 380,000, entrance fees 30,000. Payments 515,000 (next bubble).
Bar suppliers 250,000; barman wages 48,000; rent 60,000; electricity 22,000; new equipment 100,000; tournament 35,000. Total 515,000.
Closing arrears 12,000; closing advance 9,000. Credit side: 6,000 + 210,000 + 12,000 = 228,000.
Closing bar payables 21,000; closing bar inventory 45,000. Purchases = 250,000 + 21,000 − 18,000 = 253,000.
Electricity owed 3,000, so expense = 22,000 + 3,000 = 25,000. Depreciation 10% of 400,000 equipment = 40,000.
Cost or value 300,000 + 100,000 bought = 400,000. Less depreciation 40,000 = KES 360,000.
Income: subs 204,000 + entrance fees 30,000 + bar profit 84,000 = 318,000.
Rent 60,000 + electricity 25,000 + tournament 35,000 + depreciation 40,000 = 160,000. Surplus 318,000 − 160,000 = KES 158,000.
Equipment 360,000. Current assets: bar inventory 45,000 + arrears 12,000 + bank 225,000 = 282,000. Total 642,000.
Bar payables 21,000 + subs in advance 9,000 + electricity owed 3,000 = 33,000. Net assets 642,000 − 33,000 = 609,000.
451,000 + surplus 158,000 = KES 609,000. Equals net assets, so it balances.
At year end: Dr Subscriptions in arrears 12,000 / Cr Subscriptions 12,000. Dr Subscriptions 9,000 / Cr Subscriptions in advance 9,000.
Most lost marks come from mixing cash with accruals. Check these before you hand in.
Buying equipment is capital spending. It goes to the statement of financial position, not I&E. Only depreciation goes to I&E.
Show only the bar profit in I&E. Putting bar takings and purchases there as well counts them twice.
Cash received is not this year's subscriptions. Always prepare the subscriptions account or use the quick formula.
Arrears are owed to the club (asset). Advance is owed by the club (liability). Draw the T-account if unsure.
Many questions hide the opening accumulated fund. Build it from the opening balances before anything else.
Write 'surplus', 'deficit' and 'accumulated fund', not 'profit' and 'capital'. Examiners notice.
Only the yearly share goes to I&E. The rest stays in the life membership fund.
Try each one before opening the answer steps.
Opening arrears 8,000; opening advance 4,000; cash received 150,000; closing arrears 10,000; closing advance 5,000.
8,000 + 5,000 + X = 164,000, so subscriptions income = KES 151,000.
Cash 50,000; equipment 200,000; bar inventory 30,000; subs in arrears 6,000; subs in advance 2,000; bar payables 14,000.
Accumulated fund = 286,000 − 16,000 = KES 270,000.
Opening inventory 20,000; paid suppliers 140,000; payables 10,000 open, 12,000 close; closing inventory 25,000; takings 210,000; bar wages 30,000.
Gross profit 210,000 − 137,000 = 73,000. Less wages 30,000 = bar profit KES 43,000.
Five members each pay KES 30,000 for life membership. The club spreads it over 15 years.
Fund 150,000. Yearly income 150,000 ÷ 15 = 10,000. After year one the fund shows KES 140,000.

nodeData.note: How a business that makes goods works out what its goods cost to make, then links that cost to its trading and profit or loss account. Builds on Inventory and Final accounts of a sole trader.

children.note: A business that makes goods, not just buys and resells them, needs one extra account to work out what its goods cost to make.
A duka buys goods ready-made, so its cost is the purchase price. A furniture maker in Thika buys timber, pays workers and runs machines, so it must add all those costs to find the cost of each chair.
A statement prepared before the trading account. It collects all factory costs for the year and gives one figure: the cost of goods made (production cost).

manas.q: What is a manufacturing account?

children.note: It shows how much it costs to make the goods, so the owner can set prices, control factory waste and compare making with buying.

Order: manufacturing account, then trading account, then profit or loss account, then statement of financial position. The production cost passes into the trading account like purchases do for a trader.

manas.q: In what order are a manufacturer's final accounts prepared?

children.note: It is an internal working for the owners and managers. Published accounts only show cost of sales, which already includes the manufacturing costs.

IAS 2 (and IFRS for SMEs section 13) says the cost of goods made includes materials, labour and a fair share of factory overheads, but not selling or office costs. The manufacturing account follows the same idea.
Costs are built up in layers: materials, labour and direct expenses make prime cost; add factory overheads to get the cost of production.
The materials actually used up in making goods this year: opening raw materials + purchases + carriage inwards − returns out − closing raw materials.

manas.q: What is the formula for raw materials consumed?

children.note: Wages of workers who physically make the product, such as machine operators and carpenters. Also called direct wages or manufacturing wages.

manas.q: What is direct labour?

children.note: Other costs that can be traced to each unit made, such as a royalty paid per item or hire of a special machine for one job.

manas.q: Give an example of a direct expense.

children.note: The total of all direct costs: raw materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses.

manas.q: What is prime cost?

children.note: Factory costs that cannot be traced to one unit: supervisors' pay, factory rent, power, insurance, repairs and depreciation of factory machines. Also called indirect costs.

manas.q: What are factory overheads (indirect manufacturing costs)?

children.note: Goods that are started but not finished at the year end. Add opening WIP and subtract closing WIP to get the cost of goods actually completed.

manas.q: How is work in progress adjusted in the manufacturing account?

children.note: Prime cost + factory overheads + opening WIP − closing WIP. This is the cost of goods completed in the year.

manas.q: What is the formula for production cost (cost of goods manufactured)?

children.note: Office salaries, selling costs, delivery vans and finance costs do not go into the manufacturing account. They go to the profit or loss account.
Some bills cover both the factory and the office. You split (apportion) them on a fair basis given in the question.
Sharing one cost between factory and office, often by floor area or a fraction given. Only the factory part goes into the manufacturing account.

manas.q: What is apportionment of overheads?

children.note: Rent is shared 2/3 factory and 1/3 office. Factory rent = KES 120,000 (manufacturing account). Office rent = KES 60,000 (profit or loss account). Total still KES 180,000.
Depreciation on factory machines is a factory overhead. Depreciation on office computers and delivery vans goes to profit or loss.
Machine operators are direct labour. The factory supervisor is a factory overhead. Office clerks and sales staff go to profit or loss.
A manufacturer holds three types of stock at the year end, and each goes in a different place in the accounts.
Inputs not yet used, like timber and glue. Adjusted in the first part of the manufacturing account.

manas.q: Name the three kinds of inventory held by a manufacturer.

children.note: Half-made goods, such as chairs with no seats yet. Adjusted after factory overheads in the manufacturing account.
Completed goods waiting to be sold. Adjusted in the trading account, just like a trader's stock.

manas.q: In which account is finished goods inventory adjusted?

children.note: All three closing inventories appear under current assets. Many exams show them on separate lines and add them up.
IAS 2: value each at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Cost of WIP and finished goods includes a share of factory overheads.
Some firms transfer goods from factory to shop at a price above cost, to judge the factory as if it sold to an outsider.
The value at which finished goods move from the manufacturing account to the trading account, e.g. production cost plus 20%.

manas.q: What is a transfer price in manufacturing accounts?

children.note: Transfer price − production cost. It is shown at the end of the manufacturing account and added in the profit or loss account.

manas.q: How is factory profit calculated?

children.topic: Why some of it is not real
children.note: The business cannot make a profit by selling to itself. Profit in finished goods still unsold at the year end has not been earned yet.
An allowance that removes the profit hidden in closing finished goods valued at transfer price, so inventory is shown at cost.

manas.q: What is the provision for unrealised profit (PURP)?

children.note: Like the allowance for receivables: an increase in PURP is a charge in profit or loss, a decrease is added back. The full closing balance is deducted from finished goods on the balance sheet.

manas.q: How does a change in the unrealised profit provision affect profit?

children.note: If transfer = cost + 20%, the profit inside the transfer price is 20/120 (one sixth), not 20%. With 25% mark-up it is 25/125 (one fifth).

manas.q: With a 20% mark-up on cost, what fraction of the transfer price is profit?

children.note: Bidii Furniture Ltd makes sofas in Thika. All figures for the year to 31 Dec, in KES.
Opening raw materials 120,000 + purchases 850,000 + carriage inwards 30,000 − returns out 20,000 − closing raw materials 150,000 = KES 830,000.
Materials consumed 830,000 + direct labour 640,000 + royalties (direct expense) 50,000 = prime cost KES 1,520,000.
Indirect wages 180,000 + factory rent 120,000 + factory power 90,000 + machine depreciation 110,000 + factory insurance 40,000 = KES 540,000.
Prime cost 1,520,000 + overheads 540,000 = 2,060,000. Add opening WIP 100,000, less closing WIP 160,000: production cost = KES 2,000,000.
Goods are transferred at cost + 20%: 2,000,000 × 1.2 = KES 2,400,000. Factory profit = 2,400,000 − 2,000,000 = KES 400,000.
Sales 3,600,000. Cost of sales = opening finished goods 240,000 + transfers 2,400,000 − closing finished goods 360,000 = 2,280,000. Gross profit = KES 1,320,000.
Profit in opening FG = 240,000 × 20/120 = 40,000. In closing FG = 360,000 × 20/120 = 60,000. Increase = KES 20,000, charged to profit or loss.
Gross profit 1,320,000 + factory profit 400,000 − PURP increase 20,000 = 1,700,000. Less office and selling costs 700,000 = net profit KES 1,000,000.
At cost: opening FG 200,000 + production 2,000,000 − closing FG 300,000 = 1,900,000. Sales 3,600,000 − 1,900,000 = 1,700,000, the same as Step 8 before expenses.
Raw materials 150,000 + WIP 160,000 + finished goods (360,000 − PURP 60,000) 300,000 = total inventories KES 610,000.
Dr Trading account 2,400,000 / Cr Manufacturing account 2,400,000 (transfer). Dr Manufacturing account 400,000 / Cr Profit or loss 400,000 (factory profit). Dr Profit or loss 20,000 / Cr PURP 20,000.
Lay out the manufacturing account as a vertical statement, one block after another.
Opening raw materials, add purchases and carriage inwards, less returns out and closing raw materials = raw materials consumed.
Raw materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses, with a subtotal labelled prime cost.
List each factory overhead, total them and add to prime cost.
Add opening WIP, less closing WIP, to reach production cost (cost of goods manufactured).
If there is a transfer price, add factory profit to reach the transfer value carried to the trading account.
Production cost (or transfer value) replaces purchases in the trading account. Finished goods stock is adjusted there.

manas.q: What replaces purchases in a manufacturer's trading account?

children.note: These errors cost marks in KASNEB and other exams.
Putting office rent, sales staff wages or delivery van fuel in the manufacturing account. Ask: does it happen in the factory?
Carriage inwards on raw materials goes into materials cost. Carriage outwards (delivering to customers) is a selling cost in profit or loss.

manas.q: Where does carriage outwards go for a manufacturer?

children.note: Using 20% of the transfer price instead of 20/120. Mark-up is on cost, so divide by 100 + mark-up.

children.topic: Whole PURP in profit or loss
children.note: Charging the full closing PURP balance instead of only the increase or decrease for the year.
Adjusting WIP in the trading account, or before the overheads. WIP comes after prime cost and overheads.
Finished goods stock belongs in the trading account, never the manufacturing account.
Factory profit is added in profit or loss once. The trading account already uses the transfer price, so do not add it again in gross profit.
Try each one, then open the bubble for the steps.
Opening raw materials KES 40,000, purchases 300,000, carriage inwards 5,000, closing raw materials 55,000. Find raw materials consumed.
Prime cost KES 500,000, factory overheads 200,000, opening WIP 30,000, closing WIP 50,000. Find production cost.
Prime cost + overheads = 500,000 + 200,000 = 700,000.
Goods move at cost + 25%. Opening finished goods at transfer price KES 100,000, closing 150,000. Find the PURP charge.
Profit is 25/125 = one fifth of the transfer price.
Increase of KES 10,000: Dr Profit or loss 10,000 / Cr PURP 10,000. Finished goods on balance sheet = 150,000 − 30,000 = 120,000.
Classify: machine operators' wages, factory supervisor's salary, royalty per unit, fuel for the delivery van.
Operators: direct labour. Supervisor: factory overhead. Royalty per unit: direct expense. Delivery van fuel: selling cost in profit or loss.

nodeData.note: A limited company is a business that is a legal person on its own, owned by shareholders. Its accounts follow the same double entry you already know, but the owners' section (equity) is split into share capital and reserves, and the statements follow a set layout.

children.note: A business registered as a company becomes a separate legal person. It can own things, sign contracts, sue and be sued in its own name, apart from its owners.
The company is treated by law as a "person" separate from its owners. Its debts belong to the company, not to the shareholders personally.

manas.q: What does "separate legal person" mean for a company?

children.note: If the company fails, a shareholder can lose only what they paid, or agreed to pay, for their shares. Their house and personal savings are safe from company debts.

manas.q: What is limited liability?

children.note: Shareholders (members) own the company. Directors manage it day to day and prepare the accounts. In a small company the same people can be both.

A private company usually ends its name with "Limited" and cannot offer shares to the general public. A public company ends with "PLC" and may sell shares to the public, for example through the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

manas.q: What is the difference between a private and a public company?

children.note: In Kenya, companies are formed and governed under the Companies Act, 2015. It covers things like registering the company, issuing shares, paying dividends and keeping and filing accounts.

children.topic: Company vs sole trader vs partnership
children.note: A sole trader has one owner with capital and drawings. Partners share profits through current accounts. A company has share capital, reserves and dividends instead of drawings.
Most employers of accountants in Kenya are companies, from a small Ltd duka chain to listed PLCs. Company accounts are core to KASNEB exams and to daily work.
Share capital is the money owners put in by buying shares. Each share is a small slice of ownership of the company.
A share is one unit of ownership in a company. If you own 1,000 of 10,000 shares, you own 10% of the company.

manas.q: What is a share?

children.note: Ordinary shares carry voting rights and get what is left after everyone else is paid. Their dividends go up and down with profits. They are the true owners (equity).

manas.q: What are ordinary shares?

children.note: Preference shares usually get a fixed dividend (e.g. 10% of nominal value) paid before ordinary dividends. They normally have no vote.

manas.q: What are preference shares?

children.note: Redeemable preference shares will be paid back, so under IAS 32 they are usually shown as a liability and their dividend as a finance cost. Irredeemable ones are normally equity.

manas.q: How are redeemable preference shares shown?

children.note: The nominal value is the fixed face value printed on each share, e.g. KES 20. Share capital is always recorded at nominal value only.

manas.q: What is the nominal (par) value of a share?

children.note: When shares are sold for more than nominal value, the extra goes to a share premium account. It is part of equity, not profit.

manas.q: What is share premium?

children.note: Issued capital is the shares actually given to shareholders. Paid-up capital is the part of that which shareholders have paid for.
Reserves are the owners' interest other than share capital. Total equity = share capital + reserves = net assets.
Profits kept in the company over the years, after tax and dividends. It is the company version of a sole trader's profits added to capital.

manas.q: What are retained earnings?

children.note: Share premium is a capital reserve. It cannot be paid out as a normal cash dividend, but it can be used for a bonus issue.
When property is revalued upwards, the gain goes to a revaluation surplus in equity, not to profit. This links to IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment.

manas.q: Where does a gain on revaluing property go?

children.note: Directors can move some retained earnings into a named reserve, e.g. a general reserve. This is only a transfer inside equity; no cash moves.
A big reserve does not mean a big bank balance. Reserves show where the net assets came from, not what form they are held in.
Companies raise money or reshape their capital by issuing new shares. Learn the three basic types.
Dr Bank with the full cash received. Cr Share capital with the nominal value. Cr Share premium with any extra over nominal.

manas.q: What is the journal for issuing shares at a premium?

children.note: Free new shares given to existing shareholders in proportion to what they hold, paid for out of reserves (often share premium). No cash comes in.

manas.q: What is a bonus issue?

children.note: Dr Share premium (or another reserve) / Cr Share capital, at nominal value of the new shares. Total equity does not change.
New shares offered to existing shareholders for cash, in proportion to what they hold, usually at a price below market. Cash comes in.

manas.q: What is a rights issue?

children.note: Same as any cash issue: Dr Bank (cash received) / Cr Share capital (nominal) / Cr Share premium (excess).
These are the payments and charges special to a company: rewards to owners, interest to lenders, and tax to the government.
A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders. It is not an expense; it comes out of retained earnings and appears in the statement of changes in equity.

manas.q: Where do dividends appear in company accounts?

children.note: Total dividend = dividend per share x number of shares issued. Entry when paid: Dr Retained earnings / Cr Bank.
An interim dividend is paid during the year. A final dividend is proposed after the year end and approved by shareholders.
A debenture (loan note) is a written long-term loan to the company, with fixed interest. Lenders are creditors, not owners.

manas.q: What is a debenture (loan note)?

children.note: Interest is a finance cost in profit or loss, charged whether or not it is paid. Unpaid interest at year end is an accrual (current liability).

manas.q: How is loan note interest treated?

children.note: A company pays income tax on its profits (corporation tax). Entry: Dr Income tax expense / Cr Tax payable. Rates are set in Kenyan tax law: check the current KRA rate.

manas.q: How is corporation tax recorded?

children.note: IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements sets out what a full set of company accounts includes and the main lines to show.
Shows performance: revenue less costs gives profit. Main lines: revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, distribution and admin costs, finance costs, tax, profit for the year.

manas.q: What are the main lines of a company statement of profit or loss?

children.note: Shows what the company owns and owes at one date: non-current and current assets, then equity, non-current and current liabilities.

manas.q: What are the main headings of a statement of financial position?

children.note: Shows how each part of equity moved in the year: opening balance, share issues, profit, dividends, closing balance.

manas.q: What does the statement of changes in equity show?

children.note: Current items are expected to be settled or used within 12 months; the rest are non-current. Loan notes repayable after 12 months are non-current.

manas.q: When is a liability current?

children.note: Besides the three statements, a full set has a statement of cash flows and notes. Cash flows are covered in a later topic.
Many small Kenyan companies use IFRS for SMEs, which keeps the same basic statements but with simpler rules.
IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements will replace IAS 1 for periods from 1 January 2027. For now, learn the IAS 1 layout your syllabus uses.
Step by step examples in KES. Every one balances: debits equal credits, and each statement adds up.
Jamii Ltd issues 100,000 ordinary shares of KES 20 nominal at KES 30 each for cash. Cash = 100,000 x 30 = KES 3,000,000.
Dr Bank 3,000,000 / Cr Share capital 2,000,000 (100,000 x 20) / Cr Share premium 1,000,000 (100,000 x 10). Debits 3,000,000 = credits 3,000,000.
Jamii Ltd now has 100,000 shares. A 1 for 4 bonus issue gives 25,000 new shares x KES 20 = KES 500,000, paid from share premium.
Dr Share premium 500,000 / Cr Share capital 500,000. Share capital becomes 2,500,000, share premium 500,000. Total equity is unchanged.
Jamii Ltd (125,000 shares) offers 1 new share for every 5 at KES 25. New shares = 25,000; cash = 25,000 x 25 = KES 625,000.
Dr Bank 625,000 / Cr Share capital 500,000 (25,000 x 20) / Cr Share premium 125,000 (25,000 x 5). Debits = credits = 625,000.
Duka Bora Ltd issued 12% loan notes of KES 2,000,000 on 1 Jan 2025. Year interest = KES 240,000, but only KES 120,000 was paid by 31 Dec.
Dr Finance costs 240,000 / Cr Bank 120,000 / Cr Accrued interest 120,000. The full year cost is charged; the unpaid half is a current liability.
Duka Bora estimates tax of KES 450,000 and pays an ordinary dividend of KES 1.20 on 250,000 shares = KES 300,000.
Tax: Dr Income tax expense 450,000 / Cr Tax payable 450,000. Dividend: Dr Retained earnings 300,000 / Cr Bank 300,000.

children.topic: Profit or loss: Duka Bora Ltd
children.note: Year to 31 Dec 2025, in KES. Revenue 9,000,000 less cost of sales 5,400,000 = gross profit 3,600,000.
Gross profit 3,600,000 less distribution costs 700,000 and administrative expenses 1,100,000 = operating profit 1,800,000.

children.topic: Down to profit for the year
children.note: Operating profit 1,800,000 less finance costs 240,000 = profit before tax 1,560,000. Less tax 450,000 = profit for the year 1,110,000.
Opening: share capital 2,000,000, share premium 500,000, retained earnings 1,300,000; total 3,800,000. In the year 50,000 shares of KES 10 were issued at KES 16.
Share issue: share capital +500,000, share premium +300,000. Profit for the year +1,110,000 to retained earnings. Dividend paid -300,000 from retained earnings.
Share capital 2,500,000; share premium 800,000; retained earnings 2,110,000 (1,300,000 + 1,110,000 - 300,000). Total equity 5,410,000.
At 31 Dec 2025. Assets: property, plant and equipment 6,200,000; inventory 900,000; receivables 750,000; cash 410,000. Total assets 8,260,000.
Equity 5,410,000. Non-current: 12% loan notes 2,000,000. Current: payables 280,000, accrued interest 120,000, tax payable 450,000 = 850,000.
Small slips that cost marks in company accounts questions.
Never put dividends in the statement of profit or loss. They go in the statement of changes in equity, out of retained earnings.
Record share capital at nominal value. Anything above that goes to share premium, not share capital.
A final dividend proposed after the year end is not a liability at the year end (IAS 10). Disclose it in a note only.

manas.q: Is a dividend proposed after the year end a liability?

children.topic: Charge a full year of interest
children.note: Charge interest for the time the loan existed, even if unpaid. Missing the accrual is a very common error.
Unlike a sole trader, a company shows its own income tax in profit or loss and any unpaid tax as a current liability.
Owners cannot take "drawings". Money paid to owners is either salary (if they work there) or dividends.
A bonus issue only moves amounts within equity. A rights issue brings in cash. Do not mix them up.
Try each one, then open the bubble to check the steps.
A company issues 40,000 ordinary shares of KES 50 nominal at KES 65 each for cash. Give the journal.
Opening retained earnings KES 1,000,000; profit before tax 800,000; tax 200,000; dividends paid 150,000. Find closing retained earnings.
10% loan notes of KES 3,000,000 issued 1 July 2025. Year end 31 Dec 2025. No interest paid. What is the charge?
3,000,000 x 10% x 6/12 = KES 150,000. Dr Finance costs 150,000 / Cr Interest payable 150,000 (current liability).
A company has 300,000 shares of KES 10 and share premium of KES 2,000,000. It makes a 1 for 2 bonus issue from share premium.
New shares 150,000 x 10 = 1,500,000. Dr Share premium 1,500,000 / Cr Share capital 1,500,000. Share premium left: 500,000.

nodeData.note: A report that shows where a business got its cash during the year and where the cash went. It explains why the bank balance moved, and it builds on the income statement and statement of financial position you met in company accounts.

children.note: Profit and cash are two different things. A business can show a profit and still run out of money to pay rent and salaries.
Profit follows the accruals idea: sales and costs count when they happen, not when money moves. Cash only counts money actually received or paid.

manas.q: Why is profit not the same as cash?

children.topic: Example: a duka sells on credit
children.note: Mama Wanjiku sells goods costing KES 70,000 to a school for KES 100,000 on 60 days credit. Her profit is KES 30,000, yet her cash from this sale today is zero.

children.topic: Items in profit with no cash
children.note: Depreciation, allowance for receivables, and gains or losses on selling assets change profit but no cash moves at that point.
Buying a machine, taking a bank loan, repaying a loan, issuing shares and paying dividends all move cash but are not expenses or income.
Lenders, owners, investors, suppliers and managers use it to judge whether the business can pay its bills on time.
You need the income statement, the statement of financial position, depreciation, accruals and company accounts. The cash flow statement links two years of balances with one year of profit.
IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows is the international standard that tells companies how to prepare this statement. Small Kenyan entities using IFRS for SMEs follow Section 7, which works the same way.
Show every cash inflow and outflow of the year, sorted into three groups: operating, investing and financing. Then show how they add up to the change in cash.

manas.q: What does IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows require?

children.note: Notes and coins in hand plus money in bank accounts you can withdraw at once, such as a current account or M-Pesa till balance.

manas.q: What counts as cash under IAS 7?

children.note: Short-term, very liquid investments that turn into a known amount of cash with little risk of value change, usually maturing within about three months of buying them, like a 91-day Treasury bill.

manas.q: What is a cash equivalent?

children.note: An overdraft that goes up and down as part of daily cash management is deducted inside cash and cash equivalents. A long-term bank loan is not; it is financing.

manas.q: How is a bank overdraft treated in cash and cash equivalents?

children.note: Operating activities, then investing activities, then financing activities. Net change in cash, plus opening cash, equals closing cash.

manas.q: What is the basic layout of a statement of cash flows?

children.note: IFRS 18 amends IAS 7 for periods from 1 January 2027, starting the indirect method from operating profit and removing most choices on interest and dividends. Check which rules your exam sitting tests.
Every cash movement goes into one of three boxes. Ask: is it from daily trading, from long-term assets, or from the owners and lenders?
Cash from the main day-to-day trading: money from customers, payments to suppliers and staff, and usually tax paid.

manas.q: What are operating activities?

children.note: Cash received from customers, cash paid to suppliers, salaries, rent, electricity, and income tax paid to KRA.
Cash spent on or received from long-term assets and investments: buying or selling land, vehicles, machines and shares in other companies.

manas.q: What are investing activities?

children.note: A matatu firm buying a new minibus (outflow), selling an old minibus (inflow), and buying shares in a SACCO or listed company.
Cash from or to the people who fund the business: issuing shares, taking or repaying loans, paying lease liabilities and paying dividends.

manas.q: What are financing activities?

children.note: Issuing new shares for cash, receiving a bank loan, repaying loan capital, and dividends paid to shareholders.

Under IAS 7 today, interest paid may be operating or financing; interest and dividends received may be operating or investing; dividends paid may be financing or operating. Pick one and use it every year.

manas.q: Where can interest paid and dividends paid be shown under IAS 7?

children.note: Trading with customers and suppliers is operating. Long-term assets are investing. Owners and lenders are financing.
The indirect method starts with profit before tax and adjusts it back to cash. Most exam questions use it.
Start with profit before tax from the income statement. Tax and interest are dealt with separately later.

manas.q: What figure does the indirect method start from?

children.note: Depreciation reduced profit but no cash left the business, so add it back. The same goes for amortisation and impairment.

manas.q: Why is depreciation added back in the indirect method?

children.topic: Step 3: loss or gain on disposal
children.note: Add back a loss on disposal and deduct a gain. The full selling price goes under investing, so it must not be counted twice.

manas.q: How is a gain or loss on disposal treated in the indirect method?

children.note: Add back the interest charged in the income statement, then show the actual interest paid as its own line.
Adjust for movements in inventory, receivables and payables between the two year-end balances.
If inventory rose, cash was tied up in stock, so deduct the increase. If it fell, add the decrease.

manas.q: How does an increase in inventory affect operating cash flow?

children.note: If customers owe more at year end, you sold but did not collect, so deduct the increase. A fall in receivables is added.

manas.q: How does an increase in receivables affect operating cash flow?

children.note: If you owe suppliers more, you kept the cash for now, so add the increase. A fall in payables is deducted.

manas.q: How does an increase in payables affect operating cash flow?

children.note: Assets up, cash down. Liabilities up, cash up. Assets go the opposite way to cash; liabilities go the same way.
The subtotal after all the above adjustments. It is the cash the trading itself produced before interest and tax.
Interest paid = opening interest payable + interest charge - closing interest payable. With no payable, it equals the charge.

manas.q: How do you find interest paid?

children.note: Tax paid = opening tax liability + tax charge for the year - closing tax liability. Use a tax account (T-account) if it helps.

manas.q: What is the formula for tax paid?

children.note: Cash generated from operations less interest paid and tax paid gives net cash from operating activities.
The direct method lists the actual cash received and paid, line by line. IAS 7 encourages it, but the indirect method is more common.
Cash received from customers, minus cash paid to suppliers and employees, gives cash generated from operations. Both methods give the same answer.

manas.q: What is the direct method?

children.note: Opening receivables + sales - closing receivables. Use a receivables control account to find it.

manas.q: How do you find cash received from customers?

children.note: First find purchases: cost of sales + closing inventory - opening inventory. Then paid = opening payables + purchases - closing payables.
Only the operating section changes. Investing and financing are shown the same way under both methods.
Exam questions rarely give every cash figure. You work them out from movements in the statement of financial position.
Opening carrying amount - depreciation - carrying amount of disposals + purchases = closing carrying amount. Solve for purchases.

manas.q: How do you find purchases of PPE from the balances?

children.note: Opening PPE KES 800,000, depreciation 120,000, disposal carrying amount 50,000, closing 1,030,000. Purchases = 1,030,000 - 800,000 + 120,000 + 50,000 = KES 400,000.
Proceeds = carrying amount + gain, or carrying amount - loss. Asset with carrying amount KES 60,000 and gain 15,000 sold for KES 75,000.
Increase in share capital plus share premium usually equals cash received from shares issued, unless there was a bonus issue.
Fall in loan balance = cash repaid; rise = new cash borrowed. Watch for the current portion split between two lines.
Dividends paid = opening retained earnings + profit for the year - closing retained earnings, if no other movement.
Jambo Traders Ltd, year to 31 December 2025, all figures in KES thousands. We build the full statement and check it to the change in cash.
Revenue 5,000, cost of sales 3,000, operating expenses 1,100 (includes depreciation 400 and loss on disposal 20), interest 60. Profit before tax 840, tax 200, profit 640.
2025 vs 2024: PPE 3,200 / 2,600; inventory 700 / 600; receivables 500 / 550; cash 310 / 150; payables 420 / 380; tax due 180 / 150; loan 500 / 800; share capital 1,700 / 1,200.
Retained earnings: 1,370 + profit 640 - dividends 100 = 1,910. 2024: assets 3,900 = liabilities 1,330 + capital 1,200 + 1,370. 2025: assets 4,710 = liabilities 1,100 + capital 1,700 + 1,910.
A machine with carrying amount 120 was sold for 100 (loss 20). Dividends paid 100. No interest was owing at either year end.
PBT 840 + depreciation 400 + loss 20 + interest 60 = 1,320. Inventory -100, receivables +50, payables +40 gives 1,310. Interest paid -60, tax paid -170: net 1,080.
Opening tax due 150 + charge 200 - closing 180 = 170 paid.
2,600 - 400 depreciation - 120 disposal + purchases = 3,200, so purchases = 1,120.
Purchase of PPE -1,120 plus disposal proceeds +100 = net cash used in investing -1,020.
Shares issued +500 (1,700 - 1,200), loan repaid -300 (800 - 500), dividends paid -100 = net cash from financing +100.
Net change = 1,080 - 1,020 + 100 = +160. Opening cash 150 + 160 = closing cash 310, which matches the balance sheet.
Cash from customers 550 + 5,000 - 500 = 5,050. Paid to suppliers 3,060 and other cash costs 680 total 3,740. 5,050 - 3,740 = 1,310 cash generated, as before.
Most marks are lost on signs and on counting things twice. Slow down on these.
Students often add an increase in receivables. Remember: an asset going up uses cash, so deduct it.
Do not put the sale price in operating as well as investing. Only the gain or loss is adjusted in operating.

children.topic: Using the tax charge as tax paid
children.note: The charge is not the cash paid. Always adjust for opening and closing tax liabilities.
If cash includes an overdraft, opening or closing cash can be negative. Net it off before reconciling.
A bonus issue raises share capital without any cash coming in, so leave it out of financing.
Always check opening cash + net change = closing cash. If it does not match, a figure is missing or has the wrong sign.
Try each question first, then open the steps.
PBT KES 500,000; depreciation 80,000; gain on disposal 10,000; receivables up 30,000; payables down 15,000; inventory down 20,000. Find cash generated from operations.
Receivables up -30,000, payables down -15,000, inventory down +20,000: net -25,000.
570,000 - 25,000 = KES 545,000 cash generated from operations.
Opening tax liability KES 90,000, tax charge 120,000, closing liability 100,000. How much tax was paid?
KES 110,000 tax paid, shown under operating activities.
Classify: cash from customers, buying a delivery van, repaying a bank loan, issuing shares, selling an old machine.
Cash received from customers.
Buying the delivery van (outflow) and selling the old machine (inflow).
Repaying the bank loan (outflow) and issuing shares (inflow).
Opening PPE KES 1,500,000, closing 1,700,000, depreciation 250,000, asset sold with carrying amount 80,000. Find PPE bought.
KES 530,000 spent on PPE, shown as an investing outflow.
