nodeData.note: The rule book behind the rule books. It sets out why we prepare financial statements, who they are for, what makes the information useful, and when and how items are recorded. It ties together everything learned in topics 1 to 19.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A short guide to the big ideas, before the detailed concepts.
The IASB Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting is a document of basic ideas. The current version was issued in March 2018. Standards like IAS 2 and IAS 16 are built on these ideas.

manas.q: What is the IASB Conceptual Framework?

children.note: The Framework does not override any IFRS. If a standard says something different, the standard wins.

manas.q: Can the Conceptual Framework override an IFRS?

children.note: The IASB uses it to write new standards. Accountants use it when no standard covers a transaction. Auditors and students use it to understand why the rules exist.

manas.q: Name three uses of the Conceptual Framework.

children.note: Many small Kenyan businesses use IFRS for SMEs. Its Section 2 sets out the same core ideas in a shorter form.
Without shared ideas, each business could invent its own rules. A framework keeps accounts consistent and makes standards fit together.
Why financial reports exist and who reads them.
To give useful financial information about the business to investors, lenders and other creditors. They use it to decide whether to give the business money or resources.

manas.q: What is the objective of general purpose financial reporting?

children.note: Existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors. They cannot demand reports made just for them, so they rely on general purpose reports.

manas.q: Who are the primary users under the Conceptual Framework?

children.note: Employees, customers, suppliers, KRA, government and the public may also find the reports useful, but reports are not aimed mainly at them.
Users also want to know how well managers looked after the owners' resources. Good reports show whether management used money wisely.
The business, group or part of a business that prepares the reports. Its boundary decides what goes into the statements.
Reports do not show the value of the whole business. They use estimates and judgement, so they give a fair picture, not an exact one.
The qualitative characteristics: the features that make numbers worth reading. There are two fundamental ones and four enhancing ones.
Information is relevant if it can change a user's decision. It helps predict the future or confirm past guesses.

manas.q: What is relevance?

children.note: Information helps users guess future results, such as next year's sales.
Information checks or corrects earlier predictions.
An item is material if leaving it out or getting it wrong could change users' decisions. It depends on size and nature, and differs for each business.

manas.q: What is materiality?

children.note: The numbers must show what really happened. The ideal is information that is complete, neutral and free from error.

manas.q: What are the three parts of faithful representation?

children.note: Everything users need to understand the item is included, with explanations.
No bias. The figures are not tilted to look better or worse. Careful judgement (prudence) supports neutrality.
No mistakes in the process or the description. It does not mean perfect accuracy, since estimates are allowed.
Users can compare the business with last year and with other businesses. Consistent methods help this.

manas.q: Name the four enhancing qualitative characteristics.

children.note: Different independent people would agree the figure is a fair picture, for example by checking an invoice or counting stock.
Information reaches users in time to affect their decisions. Old news is less useful.
Information is clear and simple. Users are expected to have a reasonable knowledge of business and to study it carefully.
The benefit of giving information should be worth the cost of producing it.

manas.q: What is the cost constraint on useful information?

children.note: The five types of item that appear in the financial statements.
A present economic resource controlled by the business because of past events. An economic resource is a right that could bring economic benefits.

manas.q: Define an asset under the 2018 Conceptual Framework.

children.note: A present obligation to transfer an economic resource, because of past events.

manas.q: Define a liability under the Conceptual Framework.

children.note: The residual interest: assets minus liabilities. This is the accounting equation from topic 2.

manas.q: Define equity.

children.note: Increases in assets or decreases in liabilities that raise equity, other than money put in by owners.

manas.q: Define income.

children.note: Decreases in assets or increases in liabilities that reduce equity, other than payments to owners such as drawings or dividends.

manas.q: Define expenses.

children.note: Capital introduced is not income, and drawings or dividends are not expenses. They are transactions with owners.
When an item goes into the statements, and at what amount.
Putting an item into the statements. It must meet an element definition and give relevant, faithful information.

manas.q: When is an item recognised under the 2018 Framework?

children.note: Taking an item out, for example when an asset is sold or a debt is paid off.
The price paid when the item was bought, less depreciation (topic 8). Simple and easy to check.

manas.q: What is historical cost?

children.note: The price that would be received to sell an asset, or paid to pass on a liability, in a normal market deal today.

manas.q: What is fair value?

children.topic: Value in use and fulfilment value
children.note: Value in use: the present value of cash an asset will bring in. Fulfilment value: the present value of cash needed to settle a liability.
The cost to replace the same asset today, plus any transaction costs.
Profit is earned only after the opening capital is kept whole. Financial capital looks at money; physical capital looks at operating ability.
The everyday ideas used since topic 1. The Framework names some directly; others come from long practice.
We assume the business will keep running for the foreseeable future. If it will close, assets are valued at what they can be sold for.

manas.q: What is the going concern assumption?

children.note: Record income and expenses when they happen, not when cash moves. This is why topic 7 needs accruals and prepayments.

manas.q: What is the accruals concept?

children.note: Use care when judging under uncertainty. Do not overstate assets or income, or understate liabilities or expenses. Do not hide profits either.

manas.q: What is prudence?

children.note: Use the same methods each year unless a change gives better information. Changes must be explained (IAS 8).

manas.q: What is the consistency concept?

children.note: Record the economic reality, not just the legal paperwork. A leased van used like an owned one is shown as an asset.

manas.q: What is substance over form?

children.note: The business is separate from its owner. The owner's personal costs are drawings, not business expenses.

manas.q: What is the business entity concept?

children.note: Only items that can be measured in money are recorded. Staff skill or good morale is not.
Every transaction has two effects, which is the basis of double entry (topic 3).
Short KES cases showing each concept in action. Every entry balances.
A duka buys a stapler for KES 1,500 that will last years. It is too small to matter, so expense it. Dr Stationery expense 1,500 / Cr Cash 1,500.
A hospital pharmacy is owed KES 80,000 by a client who is disputing the bill and may not pay. Dr Irrecoverable debts expense 80,000 / Cr Allowance for receivables 80,000.
The same pharmacy may win KES 500,000 in a court case. Winning is not certain, so record nothing. Only disclose it in the notes if a gain is probable.
A matatu owner will close next month. Spare parts cost KES 300,000 but will sell for KES 180,000. Dr Inventory write-down 120,000 / Cr Inventory 120,000.
December power costs KES 12,000, paid in January. Year ends 31 December. Dr Electricity expense 12,000 / Cr Accruals 12,000. Profit carries the cost in the right year.
A SACCO leases a van for 5 years and uses it like its own. Under IFRS 16 it shows the van. Dr Right-of-use asset 2,000,000 / Cr Lease liability 2,000,000.
A shop owner sends KES 5,000 from the business M-Pesa till to pay school fees. Dr Drawings 5,000 / Cr Cash (M-Pesa) 5,000. It is not a business expense.
A firm switches from straight-line to reducing balance because it better matches use. Allowed, but explain the change and its effect in the notes.
Errors that cost marks.
Only relevance and faithful representation are fundamental. Comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability are enhancing.
Prudence does not allow deliberate understating of assets or creating secret reserves. That breaks neutrality.
An asset needs control, not legal ownership. Leased assets can be assets of the user.
A small item can still be material by its nature, such as a director's loan or a fraud.
If there is serious doubt about survival, the notes must explain it, even if going concern is still used.
Drawings reduce equity directly. They never go in the income statement.
Try each one, then open the steps.

children.topic: Q1: Name and explain the fundamental QCs
children.note: A typical 4-mark question.
Relevance and faithful representation.
It can change decisions through predictive or confirmatory value; materiality is part of it.
It shows the real picture: complete, neutral and free from error.
The business is closing. Which concept applies and what entry is made?
Going concern no longer applies, so use the break-up (sale) value.
Dr Inventory write-down 150,000 / Cr Inventory 150,000.

children.topic: Q3: Is a leased lorry an asset?
children.note: The lorry is on a 6-year lease and the business controls its use.
The business controls a present right to use the lorry from a past event (signing the lease).
Substance over form: control matters more than legal title.
Yes. Show a right-of-use asset and a lease liability under IFRS 16.

nodeData.note: Ratios turn the numbers in a set of accounts into simple measures of profit, cash, efficiency and risk. This topic shows how to work them out and, more importantly, what they mean.

children.note: A ratio compares two numbers from the accounts so you can see how well a business is doing. One number alone tells you little; a ratio puts it in context.
For example, profit ÷ sales tells you how many shillings of profit each 100 shillings of sales brings in. Ratios can be shown as %, as 'times', as days or as 'x : 1'.

manas.q: What is an accounting ratio?

children.note: A duka making KES 200,000 profit and a supermarket making KES 20 million cannot be compared directly. Ratios turn both into percentages so you can compare them fairly.
Owners and managers (how are we doing?), banks and SACCOs (can they repay?), suppliers (will they pay us?), investors (is the share worth buying?) and KRA (do the margins look normal?).
From the statement of profit or loss (sales, costs, profit) and the statement of financial position (what is owned and owed). You met both in final accounts and company accounts.
A ratio only means something next to another figure: last year, a similar business, the industry average or a target. This is called trend and benchmark comparison.
Profitability (are we making money?), liquidity (can we pay bills?), efficiency (how well we use stock, debtors, assets), gearing (how much borrowing) and investor ratios (return per share).

manas.q: Name the five main groups of ratios.

children.note: These ratios show how much profit the business makes from its sales and from the money invested in it.
Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100. It shows what is left from each KES 100 of sales after paying for the goods sold.

manas.q: What is the formula for gross profit margin?

children.note: Margin compares gross profit with sales; mark-up compares it with cost of sales. Margin 25% equals mark-up 33⅓%. You met this in incomplete records.

manas.q: How is mark-up different from margin?

children.note: Net profit ÷ revenue × 100. It shows what is left after ALL expenses. For a company, say whether you use profit before or after tax and stay consistent.

manas.q: What is the formula for net profit margin?

children.note: Profit before interest and tax (PBIT) ÷ revenue × 100. It shows profit from trading, before the cost of loans and tax.

manas.q: What is the operating profit margin?

children.note: PBIT ÷ capital employed × 100. It tells you how many shillings of profit each KES 100 of long-term money earns. Often called the 'main' ratio.

manas.q: What is the ROCE formula?

children.note: Capital employed is the long-term money in the business: share capital and reserves (or owner's capital) plus non-current loans. Same as total assets less current liabilities.

manas.q: What is capital employed?

children.note: Gross margin moves with selling prices, buying prices and the mix of goods sold. Net margin also moves with rent, wages and other overheads. Inventory errors also distort it.

children.topic: Liquidity: can we pay our bills?
children.note: Liquidity means having enough cash, or things soon turned into cash, to pay what is due soon. A profitable business can still fail if it runs out of cash.
Current assets ÷ current liabilities, shown as x : 1. It compares what will turn into cash within a year with what must be paid within a year.

manas.q: What is the current ratio formula?

children.note: (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. Inventory is left out because it may take a long time to sell.

manas.q: What is the quick (acid test) ratio?

children.note: Old rules of thumb say about 2 : 1 for current and 1 : 1 for quick. But a supermarket selling for cash daily can be safe with much less. Always compare with the industry.

children.topic: Too high is not always good
children.note: A very high current ratio can mean idle cash, too much stock or slow debtors. Money tied up there is not earning anything.
Efficiency (activity) ratios show how quickly stock is sold, how fast customers pay, how long we take to pay suppliers and how hard assets work.
Inventory ÷ cost of sales × 365. The average number of days goods sit on the shelf before being sold. Use average inventory if the question gives it.

manas.q: How do you calculate inventory days?

children.note: Cost of sales ÷ inventory, in times per year. It is the same idea as inventory days, turned upside down.

manas.q: What is inventory turnover?

children.note: Trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365. The average days customers take to pay. Compare it with the credit terms you give (e.g. 30 days).

manas.q: How do you calculate receivable days?

children.note: Trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365. The average days we take to pay suppliers. If purchases are not given, use cost of sales and say so.

manas.q: How do you calculate payable days?

children.note: Revenue ÷ capital employed. How many shillings of sales each shilling of long-term capital produces.

manas.q: What is asset turnover?

children.note: Operating margin × asset turnover gives ROCE. So a business can earn a good return with low margins and high sales volume, or high margins and low volume.

manas.q: How do margin and asset turnover link to ROCE?

children.note: Inventory days + receivable days − payable days. The number of days cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Shorter is usually better.
Gearing shows how much of the long-term money comes from loans rather than the owners. More borrowing means more risk.
Long-term debt ÷ (debt + equity) × 100. Some books use debt ÷ equity instead. State which one you use.

manas.q: What is the gearing ratio formula?

children.note: Highly geared = lots of loans. Interest must be paid even in a bad year, so risk is higher. Low gearing is safer but owners may miss cheap borrowing.
PBIT ÷ interest expense, in times. It shows how many times profit could pay the interest bill. Below about 2 times worries lenders.

manas.q: How is interest cover calculated?

children.note: Shareholders want to know what each share earns and what it pays out. These ratios apply to companies, not sole traders.
Profit after tax (less preference dividends) ÷ number of ordinary shares. Shown in KES per share. IAS 33 sets the detailed rules for listed companies.

manas.q: What is earnings per share (EPS)?

children.note: Market price per share ÷ EPS. It shows how many years of current earnings the market is paying for. A high P/E usually means investors expect growth.

manas.q: What is the P/E ratio?

children.note: Profit after tax ÷ dividends (or EPS ÷ dividend per share). It shows how many times the dividend could have been paid. Higher means the dividend is safer.

manas.q: What is dividend cover?

children.note: Total ordinary dividend ÷ number of ordinary shares. Compare it with the share price to get dividend yield.
A small hardware shop in Nakuru, year to 31 December 2025. All sales and purchases are on credit. Figures in KES. Every ratio below comes from these two statements.
Revenue 12,000,000. Cost of sales 8,400,000. Gross profit 3,600,000. Expenses 1,800,000. PBIT 1,800,000. Interest 200,000. Profit before tax 1,600,000. Tax 480,000. Profit for the year 1,120,000.
Opening inventory 1,200,000 + purchases 8,600,000 − closing inventory 1,400,000 = cost of sales 8,400,000.
Dividends paid in the year KES 448,000 on 1,000,000 ordinary shares. Share price at year end KES 11.20.
Assets: non-current 8,400,000; inventory 1,400,000; receivables 1,500,000; cash 300,000; total 11,600,000. Current assets total 3,200,000.
Share capital (1,000,000 shares of KES 5) 5,000,000 + retained earnings 3,000,000 = equity 8,000,000. Bank loan (10%) 2,000,000. Payables 1,200,000 + tax due 400,000 = 1,600,000. Total 11,600,000.
Opening 2,328,000 + profit 1,120,000 − dividends 448,000 = closing 3,000,000. The statement balances at KES 11,600,000.
Gross margin 3.6m ÷ 12m = 30%. Net margin 1.12m ÷ 12m = 9.3%. Operating margin 1.8m ÷ 12m = 15%. Capital employed 8m + 2m = 10m. ROCE 1.8m ÷ 10m = 18%.
Gross profit 3,600,000 ÷ cost of sales 8,400,000 = 42.9% mark-up, which matches a 30% margin.
Inventory days 1.4m ÷ 8.4m × 365 = 60.8 days. Receivable days 1.5m ÷ 12m × 365 = 45.6 days. Payable days 1.2m ÷ 8.6m × 365 = 50.9 days. Asset turnover 12m ÷ 10m = 1.2 times.
Cash cycle 60.8 + 45.6 − 50.9 = 55.5 days. Check: 15% margin × 1.2 asset turnover = 18% ROCE.
Gearing 2,000,000 ÷ 10,000,000 = 20% (debt ÷ equity = 25%). Interest cover 1,800,000 ÷ 200,000 = 9 times. Borrowing is low and safe.
EPS 1,120,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = KES 1.12. P/E 11.20 ÷ 1.12 = 10 times. Dividend per share KES 0.448. Dividend cover 1,120,000 ÷ 448,000 = 2.5 times.
Jirani is profitable (18% ROCE), can pay its bills (2 : 1), and has little debt. Watch point: customers take 46 days to pay; if terms are 30 days, credit control needs tightening.
Calculating is half the marks. The other half is saying what the ratio means, why it changed and what to do.

State the ratio, compare it (up or down from last year or the industry), give a likely reason, then say whether it is good or bad. Example: 'Receivable days rose from 38 to 46, maybe slower credit control.'
A business can show good margins but still have no cash, for example if debtors pay late or it buys too much stock. Read ratios together with the statement of cash flows.
Accounts show the past. A ratio from last year may not show what is happening today, for example after a price rise or new competitor.

manas.q: Give three limitations of ratio analysis.

children.note: The statement of financial position shows one date. Stock and debtors on 31 December may not be typical, and businesses can tidy up figures at year end (window dressing).
Two businesses may use different depreciation or inventory methods, or one revalues land. Their ratios then are not truly comparable.
Inflation makes older assets look cheap and ROCE look high. A small duka and a large chain also work very differently.
Ratios do not show staff skills, customer loyalty, location or new laws. Use them as questions to ask, not final answers.
Most lost marks come from using the wrong figure or giving no comment.

children.topic: Using total sales for receivable days
children.note: Receivable days should use credit sales. If the question says all sales are on credit, use revenue and state that assumption.
ROCE uses profit BEFORE interest and tax, because capital employed includes loans. Using profit after tax understates it.
Margin is on sales, mark-up is on cost. Mixing them up gives wrong gross profit and wrong inventory figures.
Write the formula, then the numbers, then the answer with its unit (%, times, days, : 1). Method marks come from workings.
A table of ratios alone earns few marks. Each ratio needs a short 'up/down, why, so what' comment.
Try each question first, then open the answer steps.
Current assets KES 900,000, of which inventory 300,000. Current liabilities 400,000. Find the current and quick ratios.
Revenue is KES 5,000,000 and gross margin is 25%. Find gross profit, cost of sales and mark-up.
Find receivable days and comment if credit terms are 30 days.
820,000 ÷ 6,000,000 × 365 = 49.9 days. Customers take about 50 days against 30-day terms, so credit control is weak and cash is tied up.
The loan is KES 1,500,000 and equity KES 3,500,000. Find interest cover and gearing.

nodeData.note: Communication is how we pass ideas, facts and feelings from one person to another so they are understood. For an accountant it matters as much as the numbers: correct figures are useless if the reader cannot understand or act on them.

children.note: Start here: the meaning of communication and why it matters at work.
Passing a message from one person to another so that the receiver understands it the way the sender meant it. If the meaning does not arrive, communication has failed, even if words were sent.

manas.q: What is communication?

children.note: Talking or sending an email is not enough. Communication is complete only when the other person understands and, where needed, responds.
Good communication helps staff know what to do, reduces mistakes, builds trust with customers and helps managers make good decisions.
Clear instructions mean fewer wrong payments, missed deadlines and repeated work.
Managers and owners act on what they understand. A clear report leads to better decisions than a confusing one.
Accountants explain figures, write reports and letters, answer auditors and advise owners. The skill of explaining money matters in plain words is a big part of the job.
Communication moves in steps, like a cycle. Knowing the steps helps you find where a message went wrong.
The person who has an idea and starts the communication, for example an accountant who needs a supplier invoice.

manas.q: Who is the sender in the communication process?

children.note: Turning an idea into words, numbers, pictures or gestures that the other person can receive. Choosing simple words is part of good encoding.

manas.q: What is encoding?

children.note: The actual content that is sent: what is said, written or shown.

manas.q: What is the message?

children.note: The route the message travels by: face to face, phone call, email, letter, WhatsApp, notice board or meeting.

manas.q: What is a channel in communication?

children.note: The person or group the message is meant for, for example the finance manager or a customer.
The receiver turning the message back into meaning. If the receiver does not know a term like "accrual", decoding fails.

manas.q: What is decoding?

children.note: The receiver's response that shows whether the message was understood. Feedback turns one-way sending into two-way communication.

manas.q: Why is feedback important in communication?

children.note: Anything that disturbs the message at any step: a noisy office, a poor phone network, jargon, tiredness or strong emotions.

manas.q: What is noise in communication?

children.note: The setting of the message: place, time, relationship and culture. The same words can mean different things in a boardroom and a chama meeting.
Sender, Encode, Message, Channel, Receiver, Decode, Feedback, with noise able to strike anywhere. Draw it as a loop in exams.
Messages can be spoken, written, shown by body language, or shown in pictures and charts.
Using spoken words: talks, phone calls, meetings, presentations. Quick and allows instant feedback, but leaves no record unless written down.

manas.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of verbal communication.

children.note: Letters, emails, memos, reports, minutes and notices. Gives a permanent record and suits detail, but is slower and feedback is delayed.

manas.q: Why do accountants prefer written communication for important matters?

children.note: Messages without words: facial expression, eye contact, tone of voice, posture, gestures, dress and punctuality. It can support or contradict the words.

manas.q: What is non-verbal communication?

children.note: Charts, graphs, tables, diagrams and pictures. Very useful for showing trends in figures quickly to people who dislike numbers.
Match the type to the message: urgent and simple, use a call; detailed or legal, write it; figures over time, use a chart; sensitive news, meet in person.
Messages flow in different directions inside an organisation, through official and unofficial routes.
From managers to staff: instructions, policies, targets, circulars. Risk: messages get distorted as they pass down many levels.

manas.q: What is downward communication?

children.note: From staff to managers: reports, suggestions, complaints, requests. Helps managers know what is really happening on the ground.

manas.q: What is upward communication?

children.note: Between people at the same level, for example the accounts and stores sections agreeing stock figures. Helps coordination.

manas.q: What is horizontal communication?

children.note: Between people at different levels in different departments, for example a junior accountant asking the sales manager for a sales return note.
Follows official channels and rules: memos, official letters, board reports, minutes. Reliable and recorded but can be slow.

manas.q: What is formal communication?

children.note: Unofficial talk between colleagues, over tea or on WhatsApp. Fast and friendly, but may be inaccurate and has no record.
The informal rumour network in an organisation. Very fast, partly true, and spreads when official information is missing.

manas.q: What is the grapevine?

children.note: Spreads news fast, builds team spirit and lets managers sense staff feelings.
Spreads rumours and half-truths, for example "salaries will be cut", which hurt morale.
Give staff timely, honest official information. Rumours grow where there is silence.

children.topic: Barriers and how to beat them
children.note: A barrier is anything that stops the message being understood as intended. Most barriers have a simple fix.

manas.q: What is a barrier to communication?

children.note: Technical words like "accruals" or "deferred tax" confuse non-accountants. Fix: use everyday words and explain any term you must use.

manas.q: How can an accountant overcome the jargon barrier?

children.note: Noise, distance, poor network, bad lighting, closed office doors. Fix: choose a quiet place and a reliable channel.
Anger, fear, stress or lack of interest block understanding. Fix: pick the right time and stay calm and respectful.
Different customs about greetings, eye contact, time and respect for elders can cause misunderstanding. Fix: learn and respect others' customs.
People hear what they expect. Fix: ask questions and confirm understanding instead of assuming.
Too much detail at once means key points are missed. Fix: give the main point first and the detail later.
A long report sent by SMS, or bad news by email. Fix: match the channel and time to the message.
Too many levels, rigid rules or a boss who does not listen. Fix: open-door policies and fewer layers.
A common checklist: clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous. Lists vary slightly between textbooks.

manas.q: Name the 7 Cs of effective communication.

children.note: Listening is the half of communication people forget. Hearing is just sound; listening is paying attention to understand.
Hearing happens on its own. Listening is active: you focus, interpret and respond.

manas.q: What is the difference between hearing and listening?

children.note: Fully focusing on the speaker, showing you are following, and checking you understood before you reply.

manas.q: What is active listening?

children.note: Simple habits that make people feel heard.
Put your phone away, face the speaker, keep natural eye contact.
Let the person finish before you reply or correct them.
Ask open questions like "Can you tell me more about that payment?"
Repeat the point in your own words: "So you want the invoice paid by Friday?"
Write down figures, names and dates so nothing is lost.
Daydreaming, planning your reply, prejudice against the speaker, noise and tiredness.
How the general rules apply when your daily work is figures.
An owner of a duka wants to know "Am I making money?" not the format of a trial balance. Shape the message to what they care about.
Lead with the answer, round the numbers, compare with something familiar, and use a simple chart.
Say "You made a profit of about KES 40,000 this month" before the detail.
KES 1,203,560 becomes "about 1.2 million, 10% more than last year".
Say "what the business owes (liabilities)" rather than just "liabilities".
A bar chart of monthly sales says more than a page of figures.
Payment approvals, bank instructions and changes to amounts should be confirmed in writing so there is a record.
Salaries, client accounts and tax matters must only be shared with people entitled to them. Choose secure channels.
Be polite, factual and calm in letters and emails, even when there is a dispute.
Short Kenyan workplace stories that show the process going wrong, then the fix.
Mama Wanjiku's duka sold KES 85,000 but only KES 79,500 is in the till and M-Pesa. The accountant says "there is a KES 5,500 variance due to unreconciled items."
Encoding: "variance" and "unreconciled" are jargon. Mama Wanjiku decodes it as "the accountant made an error" and gets upset (emotional noise).
Say: "Sales were 85,000 but only 79,500 came in, so 5,500 is missing. Let us check credit sales and M-Pesa together." Then ask her to repeat the plan (feedback).
The manager sends a WhatsApp: "Pay Kamau 15k." The clerk sends KES 15,000 to the wrong Kamau via M-Pesa.
The message was incomplete: no full name, phone or till number, no invoice reference. No feedback was asked for.
Use a written payment request with full name, number, amount, invoice number and approval. The clerk confirms details back before paying.
In a SACCO office, staff hear on the grapevine that salaries will be cut. Morale drops and two good clerks start job hunting.
Management stayed silent about a planned budget review, so the grapevine filled the gap with rumour.
Hold a short staff meeting and send a memo explaining the review honestly. Invite questions (upward communication).
A hospital pharmacy accountant sends a 20-page stock report. The board misses that expired drugs worth KES 120,000 were written off.
Information overload: the key point was buried on page 14.
Put a one-page summary first: "Expired drugs of KES 120,000 were written off. We recommend monthly expiry checks."
A matatu owner calls about his tax return from a noisy stage. He hears "pay 20" but the accountant said "pay by the 20th".
Physical noise and a poor channel for an important date.
Follow the call with an SMS: "Please file and pay by the 20th. Reply OK once received." The reply is feedback.
Points candidates often lose marks on.
Many answers list the process but leave out feedback. Without it there is no proof the message was understood.
Encoding is done by the sender; decoding is done by the receiver.
Noise means any interference: jargon, emotions, bad handwriting, poor network.
Examiners like balanced answers: give both advantages and disadvantages.
A barrier named without a short explanation and a fix usually earns fewer marks.

maps.title: CA12 · 2. Business letters, emails and reports

nodeData.note: How to write clear letters, memos, emails, notices and reports at work. It builds on topic 1 (Communication basics): here you put those ideas on paper or screen so the reader understands and acts.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Written business messages leave a record, travel far and can be read again. A good one saves time and money; a bad one causes confusion, delay or even a legal problem.
Any written message sent for work: letters, memos, emails, notices, circulars, reports and minutes. Its aim is to get the reader to understand and, usually, to act.

manas.q: What is business writing?

children.note: Accountants explain numbers to people who are not accountants: managers, boards, KRA, banks, SACCO members. If the writing is poor, good figures are misunderstood.
Ask three questions first: Who is my reader? What do I want them to do? What do they already know? Then pick the right format and tone.

manas.q: What three questions should you ask before writing a business message?

children.note: Seven checks for any business message. They start with the letter C so they are easy to remember. Use them to review your draft before you send it.
Use plain everyday words and one main idea per sentence or paragraph. The reader should not have to guess what you mean.

manas.q: What does "clear" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: Say it in as few words as needed, without leaving out anything important. Cut repeats and long phrases such as "at this point in time" (say "now").

manas.q: What does "concise" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: Give specific facts: names, dates, amounts, invoice numbers. "Please pay KES 184,500 by 31 October" is concrete; "please pay soon" is vague.

manas.q: What does "concrete" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: Facts, figures, names, spelling and grammar must all be right. One wrong figure in a demand letter can destroy your claim.

manas.q: What does "correct" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: Ideas follow a logical order and link smoothly, so the message reads as one connected piece. Each paragraph should lead naturally to the next.

manas.q: What does "coherent" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: The reader gets everything needed to understand and act: what, why, when, how much and who to contact. They should not need to write back to ask.

manas.q: What does "complete" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: Be polite and respectful even when complaining or chasing money. Think of the reader’s feelings and use "please" and "thank you".

manas.q: What does "courteous" mean in the 7 Cs?

children.note: A letter is a formal written message, usually to someone outside the organisation. It follows a standard layout so readers find things quickly.
Every line starts at the left margin, with no indents. Paragraphs are separated by a blank line. It is the most common modern layout.

manas.q: What is the blocked (block) style of letter layout?

children.note: Often used with blocked style: no commas or full stops in the address, date, salutation and close. Only the body text uses normal punctuation.
The standard building blocks of a business letter, from top to bottom.

manas.q: List the main parts of a business letter in order.

children.note: The sender’s printed name, logo, postal address, phone, email and website at the top of the page.
Our ref / your ref help both sides file the letter. Write the date in full, e.g. 19 October 2026, to avoid confusion.
The reader’s name, title, organisation and address, e.g. P.O. Box 12345-00100, Nairobi.
The greeting. Use "Dear Mr Otieno" if you know the name, or "Dear Sir/Madam" if you do not.
A short line in bold or capitals under the salutation saying what the letter is about, e.g. RE: OVERDUE INVOICE NO. 2041.
Opening paragraph (why you write), middle (details) and closing paragraph (what you want the reader to do next).
"Yours sincerely" goes with a named salutation; "Yours faithfully" with Dear Sir/Madam. Then the signature, name and job title.
"Enc." shows something is attached; "cc" lists others who receive a copy.
Asks for information, a price list or a quotation. Be specific about what you need and by when.
Explains a problem with goods or service calmly. State facts (dates, order number), the effect and the remedy you want.
The reply to a complaint. If the complaint is fair, apologise and say what you will do; if not, explain politely and keep the customer.

manas.q: What is an adjustment letter?

children.note: A series to recover money owed: a friendly reminder, then a firmer request asking why, then a final demand with a last date and the action that will follow. Each is firmer but stays polite.

manas.q: What are the usual stages of collection letters?

children.note: Persuades the reader to buy. A common plan is AIDA: get Attention, build Interest, create Desire, ask for Action.

manas.q: What does AIDA stand for in a sales letter?

children.note: Shorter forms used every day. Memos and emails carry most internal messages; notices and circulars reach many people at once.
A short internal written message. It has no salutation or complimentary close and is usually signed with initials.

manas.q: What is a memo and how does it differ from a letter?

children.note: To, From, Date, Subject (sometimes Ref and cc), then the message in short numbered or plain paragraphs.
Fast electronic message used inside and outside the firm. It is still a business record, so write it with the same care as a letter.
How to set up and send an email properly.
A short, specific summary, e.g. "October close delayed to 4 Nov – need approval". Never leave it blank.

manas.q: What makes a good email subject line?

children.note: To: people who must act. Cc: people kept informed, visible to all. Bcc: hidden copies, useful for big lists to protect addresses.

manas.q: What is the difference between cc and bcc?

children.note: Name the file clearly, say in the text what is attached, check it is the right version and not too big.
Polite and professional. Avoid all capitals (it reads as shouting), slang, emojis and angry replies sent in a hurry.
Greeting, main point first, details, clear request with a deadline, then a sign-off with your name, title and contacts.
Do not email payslips, patient or customer details to the wrong people. Double-check the address before you press send.
A short message put up (board, website, WhatsApp group) for many readers, e.g. an office closure. It needs a title, the key facts and who issued it.

manas.q: What is a notice?

children.note: The same letter or memo sent to many people at once, such as all members or customers. Example: a SACCO telling members about a new loan rate.

manas.q: What is a circular?

children.note: A report gives facts and analysis to help someone decide. Minutes record what happened at a meeting.
An organised written document that presents facts on a subject for a set reader and purpose, usually ending with advice.

manas.q: What is a business report?

children.note: Formal reports are long, with full headings and a title page, for boards or outside readers. Informal reports are short, often in memo or letter form.

manas.q: How does a formal report differ from an informal report?

children.note: The usual sections in order. Not every report needs all of them.

manas.q: List the main sections of a formal report in order.

children.note: Title, who it is for, who wrote it and the date.
The task given to the writer: what to look into, for whom and by when. It sets the limits of the report.

manas.q: What are terms of reference in a report?

children.note: A few lines giving the main findings and recommendations for a busy reader. Some reports call it the executive summary.
Background to the problem and how the information was collected: records checked, interviews, visits.
The facts discovered, set out under clear headings. Facts only, no opinions yet.
What the findings mean. They must follow from the findings.
Practical actions the reader should take, numbered, each linked to a conclusion.

manas.q: What is the difference between conclusions and recommendations?

children.note: Detailed tables, forms and workings put at the end so the main text stays short.
A simple route from task to finished report.
Read the terms of reference and know your reader and deadline.
Check records, ask people, observe, read earlier reports.
Group facts under headings and see what they show.
Make an outline using the standard sections, then write.
Use the 7 Cs, check every figure and name, then sign and date.
A short official record of a meeting: who attended, items discussed and decisions taken. Topic 3 covers meetings and minutes in detail.
Short model outlines in our own words, set in Kenya. Copy the shape, not the exact words.

children.topic: Payment reminder from a hospital pharmacy
children.note: Uzima Hospital Pharmacy writes to a corporate client, Baraka Logistics Ltd, whose invoice is 30 days overdue. Stage 1 collection letter in blocked style.
Letterhead, ref UHP/AR/118, date 19 October 2026, inside address, "Dear Ms Wanjiru", subject: RE: INVOICE NO. 2041 – KES 184,500.
Thank the client for their business and say that invoice 2041 dated 19 September 2026 for KES 184,500 has not yet been paid.
Assume it was missed. Give payment options: bank transfer or M-Pesa Paybill with the invoice number as account.
Ask for payment by 31 October 2026 and say to ignore the letter if already paid. Give a contact person.
"Yours sincerely" (named salutation), signature, name, Accounts Receivable Officer. Enc: copy of invoice 2041.

children.topic: Email to a manager: month-end delay
children.note: A short, clear email from an assistant accountant to the finance manager.
"October month-end close delayed to 4 Nov – bank statement missing".
Main point first: the October accounts will be ready on 4 November, not 2 November.
The bank has not sent the statement for one account, so the bank reconciliation cannot be finished.
Say you have called the bank and ask the manager to approve the new date or to escalate.
"Kind regards", name, title, phone. Cc the senior accountant who needs to know.

children.topic: Short report to a SACCO board
children.note: Outline of a report from the SACCO accountant on rising loan defaults.
The board asked on 5 October 2026 for the reasons loan defaults rose and how to reduce them, due by 31 October.
Most defaulters are new members; some guarantors were not checked; reminders are sent late.
Weak checks at approval and slow follow-up are the main causes.
1. Verify guarantors before approval. 2. Send SMS reminders 5 days before each due date. 3. Review defaulters monthly.
Table of defaulted loans by member group and month.
Errors that lose marks in KASNEB answers and cause problems at work.
Dear Sir/Madam must end "Yours faithfully"; Dear Mr Kamau must end "Yours sincerely". Mixing them is a classic lost mark.
Readers cannot see what the message is about. Always give letters a subject heading and emails a subject line.
Threats in the first reminder upset good customers. Start polite and become firmer step by step.
Findings are facts. Keep your views for the conclusions and actions for the recommendations.
Each recommendation should solve a problem shown in the findings. Random advice scores poorly.
If asked for a memo, do not write a letter. Examiners give format marks, so use the right layout and headings.
Short exam-style questions. Try them, then open the answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: Explain four of the 7 Cs
children.note: Typical short question worth about 8 marks.
Pick four, e.g. clear, concise, correct, courteous, and define each in one line.
Show each with a short work example, e.g. concise: "now" instead of "at this point in time".
You are the accountant of a supplier. A customer says they were overcharged KES 12,000. Write a suitable reply.
Blocked letter, subject heading, named salutation, "Yours sincerely".
Thank them, apologise, confirm the error, say a credit note of KES 12,000 is enclosed.
Thank them for their patience and invite further contact.

children.topic: Q3: Sections of a formal report
children.note: List and briefly explain the sections of a formal report.
Title page, terms of reference, summary, introduction/method, findings, conclusions, recommendations, appendices; one line each.
Short videos on the main ideas. They use general (not Kenyan) examples.
A quick animated tour of the seven checks for good messages.
Shows how to lay out a block style letter step by step.
A two-minute overview of the parts of a formal letter.
Practical tips for clearer, more polite work emails.

children.topic: ▶ How to write a business report
children.note: Explains the purpose and structure of a business report.
Free reading to go deeper.
Overview of business letters and their common types.

children.topic: Purdue OWL: Parts of a memo
children.note: A clear guide to memo headings and sections.
What reports are and how they are organised.
The examining body: syllabus and past papers for CPA Foundation.

nodeData.note: How to run, record and take part in meetings, and how to present figures clearly. Covers notice, agenda, minutes, roles, quorum, motions, visual aids and questions.

children.note: Meetings and talks are spoken business communication. They build on Topic 1 (the communication process) and Topic 2 (written documents), because every meeting needs written papers before and after.

children.topic: A meeting: people meeting to decide
children.note: A meeting is two or more people coming together, in person or online, to share information and agree on action.

manas.q: What is a meeting?

children.topic: A presentation: one person informing many
children.note: A presentation is a planned talk to a group, usually with slides or handouts, to inform or persuade them.

manas.q: What is a presentation?

children.note: Accountants report numbers to boards, SACCO committees, clients and staff. Good figures are wasted if you cannot explain them clearly in a room.
Formal meetings follow written rules (notice, quorum, motions, minutes), e.g. an AGM. Informal ones, like a quick team huddle, have looser rules and short notes.

manas.q: How do formal and informal meetings differ?

children.note: Board meetings, committee meetings, staff meetings, the Annual General Meeting (AGM) of members, and special or extraordinary general meetings called for an urgent matter.
A yearly meeting of all members or shareholders. They receive the accounts, elect officials and appoint auditors.

manas.q: What usually happens at an AGM?

children.note: A general meeting called between AGMs to handle an urgent or unusual matter, such as changing the by-laws.
Meetings on Zoom, Teams or Google Meet follow the same rules. Send the link with the notice, check who is present for quorum, and record decisions as usual.
Three key papers: the notice (calls the meeting), the agenda (lists the business) and the minutes (record what was decided).
A short written call telling members that a meeting will happen, with date, time, place and purpose. It must be sent within the period set by the rules.
Name of the body, type of meeting, date, time, venue or link, main business, who signs it (usually the secretary) and the date it was issued.

manas.q: List the contents of a notice of meeting.

children.note: The constitution, by-laws or law say how many days of notice are needed. A meeting called with too little notice may be invalid.
A numbered list of items to be discussed, in order. It keeps the meeting on track and lets members prepare.
1 Opening and prayer, 2 Apologies, 3 Minutes of last meeting, 4 Matters arising, 5 Main items, 6 Any other business (AOB), 7 Date of next meeting, 8 Close.

manas.q: What are the standard items on an agenda, in order?

children.note: Items that come from the last minutes, so members can check that agreed actions were done.

manas.q: What is "matters arising" on an agenda?

children.note: Small items not on the agenda. Big issues should not be sprung under AOB; they need notice.
The official written record of a meeting: who attended, what was discussed in short, and what was decided and by whom.
Record almost every word said. Used in courts and parliament, rarely in business.

manas.q: What are verbatim minutes?

children.note: A short summary of the discussion plus the decisions.
Record only the decisions (resolutions) passed, not the debate.

manas.q: What are resolution minutes?

children.note: Past tense, third person, neutral and brief. "The treasurer reported..." not "I said..." No personal opinions.

manas.q: What style should minutes be written in?

children.note: At the next meeting members check the minutes, correct errors, and the chair signs them as a true record.
Board papers or reports sent with the agenda, an attendance register, and an action list showing who does what by when.

children.topic: People and rules in a meeting
children.note: Meetings work well when people know their roles and follow simple rules on numbers, proposals and voting.
Leads the meeting: opens and closes it, follows the agenda, gives everyone a fair turn, keeps order and puts motions to a vote.

manas.q: What are the main duties of a chairperson?

children.note: If votes are tied, the rules may give the chair an extra vote to break the tie.

manas.q: What is a casting vote?

children.note: Prepares and sends the notice and agenda, keeps the register, takes and writes the minutes, and keeps records safe.

manas.q: What are the main duties of a secretary?

children.note: In clubs and SACCOs the treasurer presents the financial report, often prepared with the accountant.
Attend, read papers beforehand, speak through the chair, vote and do agreed actions.
The smallest number of members who must be present for the meeting to do valid business. The by-laws set it.

manas.q: What is a quorum?

children.note: Business done without a quorum may be invalid. The chair usually adjourns the meeting to another date.

manas.q: What happens if there is no quorum?

children.note: A motion is a formal proposal put to the meeting. Once voted and passed it becomes a resolution (a decision).

manas.q: What is the difference between a motion and a resolution?

children.note: One member proposes (moves) the motion; another seconds it to show support before debate.

manas.q: What do the proposer and seconder of a motion do?

children.note: A proposal to change the wording of a motion. It is voted on before the main motion.
Show of hands, voice vote, secret ballot or a poll. The result is recorded in the minutes.
A member asks the chair to note that the rules are being broken.

manas.q: What is a point of order?

children.note: Stopping a meeting and continuing it later, e.g. for lack of quorum or time.
A presentation has three parts: plan, deliver and handle questions. Know your audience first.
Ask: who are they, what do they already know, and what do they need to decide? A SACCO member is not a finance director.
Opening (what you will cover), body (three or four key points), close (summary and what you want them to do).

manas.q: What is the basic structure of a presentation?

children.note: Speak slowly, look at people, stand still and calm, use simple words, and keep to time.
Slides, charts, handouts, flip charts or a whiteboard help people see the message.
One idea per slide, few words, big font, and a clear title that states the point.
Bar chart to compare amounts, line chart for trends over time, pie only for a few parts of a whole.

manas.q: Which chart suits a trend over time?

children.note: Give detailed tables as a handout, not on a slide, so people can read them later.
Questions show people are listening. Plan for them and answer calmly.
List the hard questions in advance, e.g. "Why did costs rise?", and have the figures ready.
Listen fully, repeat the question so all hear it, answer briefly, then check the person is satisfied.

manas.q: What are the steps for answering a question after a presentation?

children.note: Say so honestly and promise to follow up by a set date. Never guess a figure.
Stay polite, stick to facts, and offer to discuss long issues after the session.
Rehearse aloud, time yourself and know your first sentence by heart. Some nerves are normal.
Turn numbers into meaning. Start with the story, then show only the figures that support it.
Say "about KES 12.4 million" not "KES 12,398,457.60". Exact figures go in the appendix.
A number alone means little. Compare with last year, the budget or a target.

manas.q: Why should figures be compared when presenting?

children.note: Say "money owed to us by customers" before "receivables". Explain every term once.
Show the change as a percentage and as KES, so people see both size and speed of change.
Tell the audience what the numbers mean for them and what action is needed.
Two short examples: SACCO committee minutes, and explaining a year's figures to members.
Minutes of Umoja Teachers SACCO Credit Committee held on 10 Oct 2026 at 2.00 pm, Board Room, Nairobi.
Present: 5 of 7 members (chair, secretary, 3 members); apology from 2. By-laws need 4 present, so the quorum was met.
Minutes of 12 Sep 2026 were read and confirmed as a true record. Proposed by J. Otieno, seconded by M. Wanjiru.
12 loan applications worth KES 3,600,000 were reviewed. 10 worth KES 3,000,000 were approved; 2 worth KES 600,000 were deferred for missing guarantors.
Motion to raise the maximum loan to 3 times savings. Vote: 4 for, 1 against. Carried. The secretary to inform the board.
No AOB. Next meeting 14 Nov 2026. Closed 4.10 pm. Signed: Chair ____ Date ____ ; Secretary ____.
A pharmacy shop's sales were KES 12,400,000 this year vs KES 10,000,000 last year.
Cost of goods KES 7,440,000, so gross profit = 4,960,000. Margin = 4.96m ÷ 12.4m = 40%.
"Sales grew by about a quarter, to KES 12.4 million. For every KES 100 we sold, KES 40 was left after paying for stock."
Mistakes that cost marks in KASNEB answers and cause trouble at work.
The notice calls the meeting; the agenda lists the business. They are often sent together but are not the same thing.
Business minutes should be brief and focus on decisions and actions, unless verbatim minutes are required.
Always record attendance and confirm the quorum at the start; decisions without one can be challenged.

children.topic: Too many numbers on one slide
children.note: A full trial balance on a slide loses the audience. Show three to five key figures.
When asked for minutes, include heading, present, apologies, numbered minutes and signature lines.
Try each question, then open the bubbles to check the steps.

children.topic: Q1: Notice vs agenda vs minutes
children.note: Explain the purpose of each of the three meeting documents.
Informs members that a meeting will be held and when and where.
Lists the items, in order, to be discussed.
Records attendance and decisions as the official record.
A committee has 9 members. Its by-laws say quorum is more than half. 4 members attend. Can it proceed?
More than half of 9 is more than 4.5, so at least 5 members.
Only 4 attend, which is below 5. No quorum: the chair should adjourn.
A SACCO loan book rose from KES 40 million to KES 46 million. Say it in plain words.
Increase = KES 6 million. 6 ÷ 40 = 15%.
"We lent out KES 6 million more than last year, a rise of 15%."
List four duties of the secretary of a meeting.
Issue notice and agenda, keep attendance register, take and write minutes, keep records and follow up actions.
Short videos on meeting papers, motions and presenting numbers.
Clear English guide to minute structure and phrases.
Agenda format with a worked example.
Explains making, seconding and voting on motions.
Five tips a CFO uses to make figures understandable.
Harvard Business Review on turning data into a simple story.
Free pages for definitions and the exam syllabus.
Background on what minutes are and how they are kept.
Meaning and history of the quorum rule.
How an agenda orders the business of a meeting.
Official syllabus and exam information for CPA papers.

maps.title: CA13 · 1. The legal system in Kenya

nodeData.note: How law works in Kenya: what law is, where it comes from, the kinds of law, the arms of government, the courts and ways to settle disputes without court.

children.topic: What law is and why it matters
children.note: Law is the set of rules a country makes and enforces so people can live and do business in order. This branch explains what law is for and why an accountant needs it.
Law is a set of rules of conduct, made or recognised by the state, that people must obey. If you break them, the state can enforce them through courts and penalties.

manas.q: What is law?

children.note: Law keeps order, protects people and property, settles quarrels peacefully and lets people trust each other enough to trade.
Morals are personal ideas of right and wrong; law is what the state enforces. Lying to a friend may be wrong but is not always illegal; lying on a tax return is.
Everyone, including the government and the President, is under the law and must follow it. No one can use power outside what the law allows.

manas.q: What is the rule of law?

children.note: Accountants deal with contracts, companies, tax, employees and audits every day. Knowing the law helps you spot risks, follow the rules and know which body settles a dispute.
Kenyan law comes from several places, with the Constitution at the top. The Judicature Act and Article 2 of the Constitution explain which sources courts use.
The Constitution is the supreme law and binds every person and every state organ. Any law that conflicts with it is void to the extent of the conflict (Article 2).

manas.q: Which is the supreme law of Kenya?

children.note: It was approved in a referendum on 4 August 2010 (about 67% voted yes) and promulgated on 27 August 2010.
It created 47 counties (devolution), a Senate alongside the National Assembly, a wider Bill of Rights and a more independent judiciary.
Laws passed by Parliament, such as the Companies Act or the Employment Act. They must agree with the Constitution.
Detailed rules made by a minister, county or other body using power given by an Act, for example regulations, rules and by-laws. They are void if they go beyond the parent Act.

manas.q: What is subsidiary legislation?

children.note: Common law is judge-made law that came from England. Equity is a set of fairness rules developed to fill gaps where common law was too harsh. Kenyan courts apply them where written law is silent.

manas.q: What are common law and equity?

children.note: Decisions of higher courts guide and bind lower courts in later similar cases. Supreme Court decisions bind all other courts.
Traditional rules of a community, often on marriage, land and family matters. They apply only if they do not conflict with the Constitution (Article 2(4)).

manas.q: When does customary law apply in Kenya?

children.note: Muslim law on personal status, marriage, divorce and inheritance, applied in Kadhi courts where all parties are Muslim and accept that court.
General rules of international law, and any treaty or convention Kenya ratifies, form part of Kenyan law (Article 2(5) and (6)).

manas.q: How do treaties become part of Kenyan law?

children.note: Think of a ladder: Constitution first, then Acts of Parliament, then subsidiary legislation, then common law, equity and customary law where they fit.
Law is grouped in different ways. Two key splits are civil vs criminal and public vs private.
Wrongs against society, such as theft, fraud or dangerous driving. The state prosecutes and the aim is to punish (fine or jail).

manas.q: What is criminal law?

children.note: Disputes between private persons, such as unpaid debts, broken contracts or negligence. The person harmed sues and the aim is a remedy like compensation.

manas.q: What is civil law?

children.topic: Civil vs criminal: who and what
children.note: Criminal: the Republic vs the accused, proved beyond reasonable doubt. Civil: plaintiff vs defendant, proved on a balance of probabilities.
Criminal cases need proof beyond reasonable doubt; civil cases need proof on a balance of probabilities (more likely than not).

manas.q: What is the standard of proof in civil and criminal cases?

children.note: Criminal: prosecution, accused, guilty, sentence. Civil: plaintiff, defendant, liable, damages or judgment.
Law about the state and its relationship with people: constitutional law, administrative law and criminal law.

manas.q: What is public law?

children.note: Law between private persons and businesses: contract, tort (civil wrongs), property, family and company law.

manas.q: What is private law?

children.note: Substantive law sets rights and duties (e.g. what a contract needs). Procedural law sets how a case moves through court.
The Constitution splits power between three arms so no one arm controls everything. Each checks the others.
Parliament, made of the National Assembly and the Senate. It passes Acts, approves budgets and oversees the Executive.

manas.q: What are the two houses of the Parliament of Kenya?

children.note: The lower house. Members come from 290 constituencies, plus 47 county women members, nominated members and the Speaker.
The upper house. It has one elected senator per county (47) plus nominated members and a Speaker, and protects county interests.
The President (head of state and government), the Deputy President and the Cabinet. It puts laws and policies into action.
The courts and tribunals. They interpret the law, decide cases and can strike down acts that break the Constitution.

manas.q: What is the role of the Judiciary?

children.note: Keeping the three arms apart, each with checks on the others, protects people from abuse of power.

manas.q: What is separation of powers?

children.note: Since 2010 Kenya has two levels: the national government and 47 county governments, each with its own roles.
Kenyan courts are split into superior courts and subordinate (lower) courts. Cases can move upward on appeal.
The Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal, the High Court, plus two courts with the same status as the High Court.
The highest court, set up under Article 163. It has seven judges led by the Chief Justice; five form a quorum. All courts are bound by its decisions.

manas.q: Describe the Supreme Court of Kenya.

children.note: Hears appeals from the High Court and the two equal-status courts. It has between 12 and 30 judges and is headed by a President chosen by its judges.
Set up under Article 165. It has unlimited original jurisdiction and supervises lower courts and bodies that make judicial decisions. It also hears appeals from them.

manas.q: What is special about the High Court?

children.note: Same status as the High Court (Article 162(2)(a)). It hears disputes between employers and workers, such as unfair dismissal or unpaid wages.

manas.q: Which court hears employment disputes?

children.note: Same status as the High Court (Article 162(2)(b)). It hears disputes about the environment and the use, occupation and title to land.

manas.q: Which court hears land disputes?

children.note: Courts below the High Court, set up under Article 169. Most cases in Kenya start here.
Found across the counties; they hear most civil and criminal cases. Their money limit (pecuniary jurisdiction) depends on the magistrate's rank and can be revised (check the current limit).

manas.q: What are magistrates' courts?

children.note: Decide Muslim law on personal status, marriage, divorce or inheritance where all parties are Muslim and submit to the court. Appeals go to the High Court.

manas.q: What is the jurisdiction of Kadhi courts?

children.note: A lower court for simple, low-value civil claims, meant to be quick and cheap (check the current limit).
Military courts for members of the Kenya Defence Forces. Appeals go to the High Court.
Bodies set up by Acts of Parliament to settle specialist disputes, often about decisions of government agencies, e.g. the Tax Appeals Tribunal.

children.topic: Jurisdiction – which court can hear it
children.note: Jurisdiction is a court's power to hear a case. It depends on the subject (land, labour, family), the amount of money, and the place.

manas.q: What is jurisdiction?

children.note: A party unhappy with a decision may appeal to a higher court: lower courts → High Court (or ELRC/ELC) → Court of Appeal → Supreme Court.
The Chief Justice heads the Judiciary and chairs the Judicial Service Commission. The Chief Registrar is its chief administrator and accounting officer.
Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) means ways of settling disputes without a full court case. Article 159 tells courts to promote it.

children.topic: What ADR is and why use it
children.note: Ways to settle a quarrel outside a full trial. Often cheaper, faster, private and better for keeping a business relationship.
The parties talk directly and agree a solution themselves, with no outsider.
A neutral person (mediator) helps the parties reach their own agreement. The mediator does not impose a decision.

manas.q: What is mediation?

children.note: A neutral person helps restore the relationship and may suggest terms, but the parties decide.
The parties choose an arbitrator who hears both sides and makes a binding decision called an award. Contracts often include an arbitration clause.

manas.q: What is arbitration?

children.note: Community methods, like a council of elders, recognised by Article 159. They must not break the Bill of Rights or the Constitution.
Courts must do justice to all, avoid delay, and promote reconciliation, mediation, arbitration and traditional methods.
Short real-life style cases showing how to decide what kind of law applies and where the matter goes.
A matatu driver speeds and injures a passenger. Two separate matters can follow: a criminal one and a civil one.
The state (prosecution) charges the driver with a traffic offence in a magistrates' court. The aim is punishment: a fine or jail.
The passenger sues the matatu owner for, say, KES 400,000 compensation for medical bills. She must prove her case on a balance of probabilities.
A duka owner owes a wholesaler KES 150,000. This is civil (contract). The wholesaler can first negotiate, then sue in a magistrates' court or the Small Claims Court (check the current limit).
A hospital pharmacy dismisses a cashier without a hearing. She claims unfair dismissal. This goes to the Employment and Labour Relations Court, not the ordinary High Court.
Two neighbours in Kiambu argue over who owns a strip of land. A dispute over land title belongs to the Environment and Land Court system.

children.topic: Case 5: inheritance in a Muslim family
children.note: All heirs are Muslim and agree to Islamic law. The Kadhi court can decide shares. If one heir is unhappy, the appeal goes to the High Court.
A SACCO and a software firm agreed to arbitrate any dispute. When the system fails, they go to an arbitrator, whose award binds both sides.
Easy places to lose marks on this topic.

children.topic: Calling the High Court the highest
children.note: The Supreme Court is the highest court in Kenya, not the High Court.
Do not say a defendant in a civil case is "guilty"; say "liable". The accused in a criminal case is "convicted".
No. It applies only where it does not conflict with the Constitution or written law.
Kadhi courts only hear Muslim personal matters where all parties are Muslim and submit to them; they do not hear criminal cases.
The ELRC and the Environment and Land Court have the same status as the High Court; list them under superior courts.
A mediator helps parties agree; an arbitrator decides. Only arbitration ends in a binding award.
Court money limits change by gazette notice. In practice, always check the current limit before filing.

children.topic: Q1: List five sources of Kenyan law
children.note: A common opening question in this paper.
Constitution 2010; Acts of Parliament; subsidiary legislation; common law and equity; African customary law; Islamic law; international law and ratified treaties. Explain each in one line.

children.topic: Q2: Civil vs criminal – four differences
children.note: Compare the two kinds of law.
Parties (state vs accused / plaintiff vs defendant); purpose (punish / compensate); standard of proof (beyond reasonable doubt / balance of probabilities); outcome (sentence / damages).
Name and describe each superior court.
Supreme Court (top, Article 163); Court of Appeal (appeals); High Court (unlimited original jurisdiction, Article 165); ELRC and ELC (same status as High Court, Article 162(2)).
Explain the difference with an example.
Mediation: neutral helps parties agree, no imposed decision. Arbitration: arbitrator hears both and gives a binding award. Example: a supplier contract with an arbitration clause.
