nodeData.note: How promises become legally binding in Kenya: the building blocks, terms, what spoils a contract, how it ends and what you can claim when it is broken.

children.note: A contract is a promise, or set of promises, that the law will enforce. If one side breaks it, the other side can go to court.
An agreement between two or more people that the law will enforce.

manas.q: What is a contract?

children.note: Sales, purchases, loans, leases, jobs and audit engagements are all contracts. Revenue and debts in the books rest on them.

children.topic: Where Kenyan contract law comes from
children.note: The Law of Contract Act (Cap 23) applies the English common law of contract in Kenya, with some changes. So English cases are taught and followed.

manas.q: Which Act applies English contract law in Kenya?

children.note: Contract law is part of private civil law. Disputes go to the civil courts, and English cases act as persuasive precedent.
Every contract is an agreement, but not every agreement is a contract. A promise to meet a friend for lunch is not enforceable.
Valid: fully binding. Void: no contract at all. Voidable: binding until the innocent party cancels it. Unenforceable: valid but cannot be sued on, e.g. missing writing.

manas.q: What is the difference between void and voidable contracts?

children.note: A valid contract needs: offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity, legality and certainty. Miss one and there is no binding contract.
A clear promise to be bound on stated terms as soon as the other person says yes.

manas.q: What is an offer?

children.note: An invitation to treat only invites offers: shop displays, price lists, adverts, auctions. The customer makes the offer; the shop may accept or refuse.

manas.q: What is an invitation to treat?

children.note: A shopkeeper showed a flick knife with a price ticket in his window. He was charged with offering it for sale, but the court held a window display is only an invitation to treat.
In Pharmaceutical Society v Boots, goods on a self-service shelf were held to be an invitation to treat. The contract is made at the till.

children.topic: Case: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball (1893)
children.note: The company promised £100 to anyone who caught flu after using its smoke ball as directed. Mrs Carlill did and got flu. The advert was a unilateral offer to the world, accepted by doing what it asked.
Rejection, counter-offer, revocation before acceptance, lapse of time, death, or failure of a condition.
A final, unconditional yes to all the terms of the offer, communicated to the offeror.

manas.q: What is acceptance?

children.note: Changing the terms is a new offer, not acceptance. In Hyde v Wrench, a reply offering £950 for a farm offered at £1,000 destroyed the original offer.

manas.q: What is the effect of a counter-offer?

children.note: You cannot force a contract by saying "if I hear nothing, we have a deal".
Acceptance sent by post is complete when the letter is posted, not when it arrives, if post was a reasonable way to reply. From Adams v Lindsell (1818).

manas.q: What is the postal rule?

children.note: For phone, email, WhatsApp and similar near-instant methods, the normal rule applies: acceptance counts when received.
Each side must give something of value in return: money, goods, a service, or a promise. A bare promise of a gift is not enforceable.

manas.q: What is consideration?

children.note: Gave the classic definition: consideration is a benefit to one side or a loss or burden taken on by the other.
It need not be adequate (a fair price) but must be sufficient (have some value). Past consideration does not count. It must move from the promisee.
Both sides must mean the deal to be legally binding.

manas.q: What is intention to create legal relations?

children.note: In Balfour v Balfour a husband promised his wife £30 a month while apart. The court held there was no contract: domestic deals are presumed not legally binding.
Commercial deals are presumed binding unless clearly stated otherwise, e.g. "binding in honour only".
The legal ability to make a contract. Minors (under 18 in Kenya), people of unsound mind and drunk persons have limited capacity.

manas.q: Who lacks full capacity to contract?

children.note: The purpose must be lawful. A deal to smuggle goods or bribe an officer is illegal and the courts will not enforce it.
Terms must be clear enough for a court to know what was agreed. "Supply maize at a fair price someday" is too vague.
Terms are the promises inside the contract. Some are key, some minor; some limit liability.
Express terms are stated in words. Implied terms are filled in by law, custom or business sense, e.g. goods sold must be fit for purpose.
A main term going to the root of the contract. If broken, the innocent party may end the contract and claim damages.

manas.q: What is a condition?

children.note: A lead singer fell ill and missed the opening nights of an opera. This broke a condition, so the producers could end her contract.
A minor side term. If broken, the innocent party can claim damages only, not end the contract.

manas.q: What is a warranty?

children.note: A singer arrived late for rehearsals but was ready to perform. This broke only a minor term, so the employer could not end the contract.
Some terms are judged by how serious the effect of the breach was, not by their label.
A clause that limits or removes one side’s liability, e.g. "We are not liable for loss of goods in our store".

manas.q: What is an exemption clause?

children.topic: Must be part of the contract
children.note: By signing (L'Estrange v Graucob: you are bound by what you sign), by clear notice before the deal, or by past dealings.
Courts read unclear exemption clauses against the party relying on them. Consumer protection law also limits unfair clauses.
Even with all the essentials, some problems make a contract void or voidable.
A false statement of fact that persuades someone to enter the contract. The contract is voidable.

manas.q: What is misrepresentation?

children.note: Fraudulent (knowingly false), negligent (careless) and innocent (honest belief). Fraud gives the strongest remedies.
Rescission (undo the contract and restore both sides) and/or damages, depending on the type.
Usually a mistake does not affect a contract. Only a basic shared mistake, e.g. the goods no longer exist, can make it void.
Making someone agree by threats of violence or unlawful pressure on their business. The contract is voidable.

manas.q: What is duress?

children.note: Unfair use of a position of trust, e.g. doctor and patient, or lawyer and client. The contract is voidable.

manas.q: What is undue influence?

children.note: A contract to do something illegal or against public policy is void, and courts will not help either side.
A contract ends when duties are released: by performance, agreement, frustration or breach.

manas.q: What are the four ways a contract is discharged?

children.note: Both sides do exactly what they promised. Normally performance must be complete; part performance rarely earns full payment.
Both sides agree to end or change the contract, each giving up something.
An event after the contract, not anyone’s fault, makes performance impossible or pointless. Both are released.

manas.q: What is frustration of contract?

children.note: A music hall rented for concerts burned down a week before the first concert. The contract was ended by impossibility; neither side was liable.
Rooms were rented to view the coronation of Edward VII, which was postponed. The purpose failed, so the contract was frustrated.
One side fails to perform, performs badly, or says in advance they will not perform (anticipatory breach).

manas.q: What is anticipatory breach?

children.note: What the innocent party can get from the court: damages, specific performance or an injunction.
Money to put the innocent party where they would have been if the contract had been performed.

manas.q: What is the aim of contract damages?

children.note: A carrier delivered a mill’s broken crankshaft late. The mill lost profit, but the court refused that loss: only losses that are natural or known to both sides are recoverable.

manas.q: What rule does Hadley v Baxendale set?

children.note: The innocent party must take reasonable steps to cut the loss, e.g. buy elsewhere quickly.
A fair pre-agreed sum for breach, e.g. KES 5,000 per day of delay. A penalty set only to scare is not enforced.
A court order to actually do the contract. Used where money is not enough, e.g. sale of land. It is discretionary.

manas.q: What is specific performance?

children.note: A court order stopping someone from doing something, e.g. breaking a promise not to work for a rival.
Undoing the contract and putting both sides back where they started; common for misrepresentation.

children.topic: Contracts that must be in writing
children.note: Most contracts can be oral. The Law of Contract Act (Cap 23) requires some to be in writing.
A contract to sell or dispose of an interest in land must be in writing, signed by all parties and witnessed.

manas.q: Under Cap 23, what land contracts must be in writing?

children.note: A promise to pay another person’s debt (guarantee) cannot be sued on unless in writing and signed by the guarantor.

manas.q: Which promise about another person's debt must be in writing?

children.note: Accountants handling loans, SACCO guarantors and property deals should check the paperwork is signed and witnessed.
Simple cases with KES figures to practise the rules.
Mama Akinyi agreed to buy 1,000 bags at KES 3,000 (total KES 3,000,000). The seller failed; she bought elsewhere at KES 3,400.
Extra transport to fetch the new maize: KES 20,000. Total so far KES 420,000.
She also lost a KES 150,000 export deal the seller never knew about. Under Hadley v Baxendale it is too remote.
Damages = KES 400,000 + KES 20,000 = KES 420,000.
A phone is tagged KES 1,500 instead of KES 15,000. The tag is an invitation to treat, so the shop can refuse the customer’s offer.
Otieno posts acceptance of an offer to buy a matatu for KES 2,800,000 on Monday. Seller revokes by phone Tuesday; letter arrives Wednesday. Contract made Monday (postal rule).
A builder agreed KES 10,000 per day of delay. He is 12 days late: 12 × 10,000 = KES 120,000 payable.
Errors candidates often make in this topic.
Shop displays, adverts and price lists are usually invitations to treat. Carlill is the exception: a unilateral offer.
The postal rule applies to acceptance only. A revocation counts only when it actually reaches the offeree.
Consideration need not be a fair price; it only needs some value.
Breach of condition: end + damages. Breach of warranty: damages only.
A deal becoming more costly is not frustration. It must be impossible or pointless.
Short exam-style questions with answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: Is a shop display an offer?
children.note: Explain with a case.
Define offer and invitation to treat. Apply Fisher v Bell or Boots. Conclude the customer offers at the till.
Supplier fails to deliver 500 crates at KES 800; market price is KES 950.
500 × (950 − 800) = KES 75,000. State the aim of damages and mention mitigation and remoteness.

children.topic: Q3: List the ways to discharge
children.note: Name and explain four ways a contract ends.
Performance, agreement, frustration (Taylor v Caldwell), breach. One line each with an example.

maps.title: CA13 · 3. Agency, sale of goods and partnerships

nodeData.topic: Agency, sale of goods and partnerships
nodeData.note: Three everyday areas of business law built on the law of contract: acting for someone else (agency), buying and selling goods, and running a business with partners. Accountants meet all three daily.

children.note: These rules decide who must pay, who owns the goods and who carries a loss. Accountants use them when recording sales, chasing debts and advising partners.
Agency, sale of goods and partnership are all special kinds of contract. Offer, acceptance, consideration and capacity from topic 2 still apply.
Kenya has a Sale of Goods Act, a Partnerships Act and the Limited Liability Partnership Act (No. 42 of 2011). Agency rules come mainly from common law (court cases).
Agency is a relationship where one person (the agent) is allowed to act for another (the principal) and make contracts that bind the principal with outsiders (third parties).
The principal gives the power, the agent uses it, and the third party deals with the agent. Once the deal is made, the contract is usually between principal and third party.
Agency can arise in five main ways: by express agreement, by implication, by necessity, by ratification (approving later) and by estoppel (appearing to give authority).
The principal clearly appoints the agent, in words or writing. A written power of attorney is a formal example.

manas.q: What is express agency?

children.note: The relationship is understood from conduct or the situation, e.g. a shop manager is taken to have power to buy normal stock.
In an emergency a person acts to protect another's goods without prior permission. Usually needs: a real emergency, no way to contact the owner, and acting in good faith.

manas.q: What conditions are needed for agency of necessity?

children.note: The principal adopts a contract made without authority. The agent must have said they acted for that principal, who existed and had capacity at the time.

manas.q: What is ratification in agency?

children.topic: Estoppel: you made it look real
children.note: If the principal leads a third party to believe someone is their agent, the principal cannot later deny it when the third party relied on it.
Authority is how far the agent can go. A principal is bound when the agent acts within actual or apparent authority.
Real power given by the principal, either expressly stated or implied as normal for that job.

manas.q: What is actual authority?

children.note: Power the agent seems to have because of how the principal presented them. It protects an outsider who reasonably relied on that appearance.

manas.q: What is apparent authority?

children.note: An agent is trusted with the principal's affairs, so the law expects loyalty and care.
Do what was agreed, within the limits set. Going beyond them can make the agent liable for loss.
Work as carefully as a reasonable person in that role. A professional agent must show professional skill.
The agent should not hand the job to someone else without permission, because the principal chose them.
Do not put own interest against the principal and do not keep hidden commissions or bribes. Any secret profit belongs to the principal.

manas.q: What happens to a secret profit made by an agent?

children.note: Keep the principal's money separate and account for every shilling received and spent.
The principal must pay the agreed commission or fee, and repay (indemnify) the agent for proper expenses and losses incurred while acting within authority.

manas.q: What are the principal's main duties to an agent?

children.note: Agency ends by the parties' own act or by operation of law.
Mutual agreement, the principal withdrawing authority (revocation), the agent giving up (renunciation), or the job being completed or time running out.
Death, insanity or bankruptcy of either party, or the work becoming illegal or impossible (frustration).
A contract of sale of goods is one where the seller transfers, or agrees to transfer, ownership of goods to the buyer for money called the price. Kenya's Sale of Goods Act sets the default rules.
In a sale, ownership passes now. In an agreement to sell, ownership passes later or after a condition is met; it becomes a sale when that happens.

manas.q: What is the difference between a sale and an agreement to sell?

children.note: Existing goods (owned now) or future goods (to be made or acquired). Specific goods are identified at the time of the contract; unascertained goods are not yet picked out.

manas.q: What are specific goods vs unascertained goods?

children.note: A condition is a key term: breach lets the buyer reject the goods and claim damages. A warranty is a minor term: breach gives damages only.

manas.q: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty?

children.note: Even if not written, the Act reads certain promises into the contract to protect buyers.
Seller must have the right to sell. Buyer should also enjoy quiet possession and goods free from hidden charges.

manas.q: What is the implied term as to title?

children.note: Where goods are sold by description, they must match it. "Grade 1 Basmati rice" must not be grade 3.
Where the seller deals in such goods, they should be of merchantable (saleable) quality, and fit for a purpose the buyer made known and relied on the seller for.

manas.q: When is there an implied term of fitness for purpose?

children.note: The bulk must match the sample, the buyer should get a fair chance to compare, and goods must have no hidden defect not visible in the sample.
Ownership ("property") passes when the parties intend it to. If they say nothing, the Act gives rules.
Ownership usually passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is later.

manas.q: When does property pass in specific goods in a deliverable state?

children.topic: Seller still has work to do
children.note: If the seller must do something to put goods in a deliverable state, or weigh or measure them to fix the price, ownership passes once done and the buyer is told.

children.topic: On approval or sale or return
children.note: Ownership passes when the buyer signals acceptance, or keeps the goods past the agreed or a reasonable time.
Ownership cannot pass until the goods are picked out and set aside for this buyer with both sides' consent.
A seller can keep ownership until paid in full, even after delivery. Useful protection when selling on credit.
The general rule is risk follows ownership: whoever owns the goods bears accidental loss, unless the parties agree otherwise or delivery was delayed by one side's fault.

manas.q: What is the general rule on passing of risk?

children.topic: Selling what you do not own
children.note: Normally no one can pass better ownership than they have (nemo dat). There are exceptions, such as sale by a mercantile agent or a seller still in possession.

manas.q: What does the nemo dat rule mean?

children.note: A seller not fully paid has rights over the goods themselves, as well as the right to sue the buyer.
A seller still holding the goods may refuse to release them until paid. The lien is lost once goods reach the buyer.

manas.q: What is an unpaid seller's lien?

children.note: If the buyer becomes insolvent while goods are with a carrier, the seller can order the carrier to stop and return them.

manas.q: When can an unpaid seller stop goods in transit?

children.note: Where goods are perishable, or the seller gives notice and the buyer still does not pay, the seller may resell and claim any shortfall.
Action for the price where ownership has passed, or damages for non-acceptance where the buyer wrongly refuses the goods.
A partnership is a relationship between people carrying on a business together with a view to making profit. Kenya's Partnerships Act governs it.
Two or more persons, a business, carried on in common, aiming for profit. Simply sharing gross income does not on its own make people partners.

manas.q: Define a partnership.

children.note: A written agreement setting capital, profit-sharing ratio, salaries, interest and how to leave. Where silent, default rules in the law apply.
Rules that apply when the agreement says nothing.

children.topic: Equal share of profits and losses
children.note: With no agreement, partners share profits and bear losses equally, whatever capital each put in.

manas.q: How are profits shared if the partnership agreement is silent?

children.topic: No salary, no interest on capital
children.note: No partner gets a salary or interest on capital unless agreed. Loans beyond agreed capital may earn interest.
Every partner may take part in running the business and inspect the books.
A new partner or a change in the nature of the business needs all partners to agree. Ordinary matters go by majority.
Partners must act in utmost good faith toward each other.
Give full and honest information on anything affecting the firm.
A partner must hand over profit made from firm business, property or name without the others' consent.
A partner must not run a competing business without consent; profits from it belong to the firm.

manas.q: What happens if a partner secretly runs a competing business?

children.note: Each partner is an agent of the firm, so acts done in the usual way of business bind all partners.
Partners are liable for firm debts beyond the firm's assets, out of their own pockets. A creditor can pursue the partners for the whole debt.

manas.q: How are partners liable for firm debts?

children.note: A person who lets others believe they are a partner can be liable as one to those who relied on it.
A new partner is usually not liable for debts from before joining. A retiring partner stays liable for old debts and should give notice to avoid new ones.
Under Kenya's Limited Liability Partnership Act (No. 42 of 2011) an LLP, once registered, is a legal person separate from its partners.
Registration by the Registrar of Companies gives the LLP its own legal personality, so it can own property and be sued in its own name.

manas.q: What gives a Kenyan LLP its legal personality?

children.note: A partner's liability is generally limited to capital still unpaid. A partner can still be liable for their own acts done without authority.
The partnership can end by the partners' choice, automatically by events, or by court order.
Ends on the date in the deed, when the venture is finished, or by notice in a partnership at will.
Death or bankruptcy of a partner (unless the deed says otherwise), or the business becoming illegal.
For example permanent incapacity, serious misconduct, a business that can only run at a loss, or where it is just and fair to end it.

manas.q: Give grounds on which a court may dissolve a partnership.

children.note: Outside creditors first, then partners' loans, then partners' capital, then any surplus in profit-sharing ratio.

manas.q: In what order are assets applied on dissolution?

children.note: Short cases with numbers you can check.
Agent sells 40 bags at KES 4,500 = KES 180,000. Commission 5% = KES 9,000. Agent pays the farmer KES 180,000 − 9,000 = KES 171,000.
The buyer also slips the agent KES 15,000. That is a secret profit: the farmer can claim the KES 15,000 and may refuse the KES 9,000 commission.
Wanjiku buys a specific fridge for KES 60,000, pays KES 20,000, collects tomorrow. A fire destroys it overnight. Ownership and risk passed at contract, so she still owes KES 40,000.
100 bags at KES 750 = KES 75,000, unpaid. After notice the seller resells at KES 650 = KES 65,000. Seller claims the shortfall: 75,000 − 65,000 = KES 10,000.
Profit KES 900,000. Baraka gets salary KES 120,000. Remaining KES 780,000 shared 3:2:1 = Amani 390,000, Baraka 260,000, Chebet 130,000. Baraka total KES 380,000.
Same KES 900,000 profit but no agreement: no salary, equal shares. Each of the 3 partners gets KES 300,000.
Firm owes KES 600,000; firm assets cover KES 240,000. Shortfall KES 360,000. The creditor may chase any partner; among themselves 3:2:1 = 180,000, 120,000, 60,000.
Partner agreed capital KES 500,000, paid KES 300,000. Her further liability for LLP debts is generally the unpaid KES 200,000.
Points examiners like to test.
Even if the principal privately limited the agent, an outsider who relied on the appearance may still bind the principal.
The buyer can bear the loss even before taking delivery, if ownership has passed.
Once goods reach the buyer, the seller can no longer keep them; stoppage in transit only works while with a carrier.
With no agreement, profits split equally, even if one partner put in more capital.
Only a registered LLP is a separate legal person with limited liability. Ordinary partners pay debts from personal assets.
Try each question first, then open the steps.

children.topic: Q1: Did the manager bind the firm?
children.note: A shop manager, told privately not to buy on credit, buys stock on credit from a regular supplier. Is the owner bound?
No: the owner forbade credit buying.
Yes: managers usually buy stock and the supplier did not know of the limit.
The owner is bound to pay; the manager may be liable to the owner for disobeying.

children.topic: Q2: Can the seller stop the lorry?
children.note: Seller ships goods by lorry; buyer is declared bankrupt before arrival. Advise the seller.
Yes, the price is unpaid.
Yes, with an independent carrier and not yet delivered.
Seller may stop the goods in transit and get them back, then resell.
A, B, C share profits 2:2:1. Loss KES 250,000. No other terms. How is it shared?
Losses follow the agreed profit ratio of 2:2:1, total 5 parts.

nodeData.note: How a company or organisation is directed and kept in check, so the people running it act for the people who own it and others who depend on it. This builds on agency and partnerships from topic 3.

children.topic: What governance is and why it matters
children.note: Governance is the system of rules and people that steers an organisation and checks the managers. Good governance protects owners, staff, lenders and the public.
The way a company is directed and controlled: who holds power, how decisions are made and how performance is watched by the board, managers and shareholders.

manas.q: What is corporate governance?

children.note: In a big company the owners (shareholders) do not run the business day to day. They hire directors and managers to run it for them.
Managers (agents) may follow their own interests instead of the owners' (principals) interests, for example big bonuses or easy jobs. Recall agency from topic 3.

manas.q: What is the agency problem in corporate governance?

children.note: Managers know far more about the business than shareholders do. This gap (asymmetric information) makes it hard for owners to check managers.
The money lost or spent because agents and principals differ: losses from bad manager choices plus the cost of checks such as audits and reports.

manas.q: What are agency costs?

children.note: Anyone affected by the organisation: shareholders, staff, customers, suppliers, lenders, the community and government (KRA).

manas.q: Who are stakeholders?

children.note: The shareholder view says run the company mainly for owners. The stakeholder view says balance the needs of all groups affected by it.
Good governance builds trust, makes it easier to raise money, cuts fraud and helps the organisation last. Poor governance can collapse even huge firms.
Most governance codes rest on a few simple ideas. An easy way to remember them: ATFR.
Those who hold power must answer for how they used it. The board answers to shareholders; managers answer to the board.

manas.q: What does accountability mean in governance?

children.note: Being open: sharing clear, timely and true information, such as honest financial statements and disclosure of conflicts.

manas.q: What does transparency mean in governance?

children.note: Treating all shareholders and stakeholders equally and justly, including small (minority) shareholders.

manas.q: What does fairness mean in governance?

children.note: The board and managers act with care, obey the law and consider the effect of decisions on society and the environment.

manas.q: What does responsibility mean in governance?

children.note: Many codes also stress integrity (honesty), independence of judgement and probity. They support the four main principles.
A rules-based system sets fixed laws everyone must obey. A principles-based system sets broad aims and often lets firms "comply or explain" why they did not.
The board sits between the owners and the managers. It sets direction, appoints and checks top managers and answers to shareholders.
Sets strategy, approves budgets, appoints the CEO, checks risks and controls, and reports to owners.
Directors who are also full-time managers of the company, such as the CEO or finance director.

manas.q: Who is an executive director?

children.note: Directors who sit on the board but do not manage the business day to day. They bring outside views and challenge managers.

manas.q: Who is a non-executive director?

children.note: NEDs with no close ties to the company, its managers or big shareholders, so their judgement is free. Examples of lost independence: recent employee, big supplier, family of the CEO.

manas.q: What makes a director independent?

children.note: The chair runs the board; the CEO runs the business. Splitting the two jobs stops one person holding too much power.

manas.q: Why separate the chair and CEO roles?

children.note: Smaller groups of directors who look closely at one area and report back to the full board.
Mostly independent NEDs. Oversees financial reporting, internal controls, internal audit and the external auditor.

manas.q: What does the audit committee do?

children.note: Finds and proposes new directors and plans for succession, so the board has the right mix of skills.

manas.q: What does the nomination committee do?

children.note: Sets the pay of directors and top managers. No director should decide their own pay.

manas.q: What does the remuneration committee do?

children.note: Some boards also keep a risk committee to watch the main risks the organisation faces.
Boards should review their own performance regularly and keep directors trained and up to date.
Audits check the numbers and the controls; ethics guides behaviour when no rule covers the case.
Staff (or hired firm) inside the organisation who test controls and processes all year and report to the audit committee.

manas.q: What is internal audit?

children.note: An independent auditor appointed by shareholders who gives an opinion on whether the financial statements are fairly presented.

manas.q: What is external audit?

children.note: Internal audit serves management and the board and covers any area; external audit serves shareholders and focuses on the financial statements.
Auditors must be free of links that cloud judgement, such as owning shares in the client or doing too much other work for it.
When a person's private interest (family, business, money) clashes with their duty to the organisation.

manas.q: What is a conflict of interest?

children.note: Declare it at once, record it in the minutes, leave the room and do not vote on the matter. Keep a register of interests.
Act honestly, keep secrets you are trusted with, refuse bribes and gifts meant to sway you, and speak up about wrongdoing.
Reporting wrongdoing through a safe channel. Good organisations protect people who report in good faith.

manas.q: What is whistleblowing?

children.note: Kenya has laws and regulators that push for good governance in both private companies and public bodies.
The government body that licenses and supervises Kenya's capital markets, including the stock exchange and market players, under the Capital Markets Act.

manas.q: What does the Capital Markets Authority of Kenya do?

children.note: Companies whose shares trade on the stock exchange must follow CMA guidelines on boards and disclosure. Check the current CMA governance code in your study pack.
The supreme law, promulgated on 27 August 2010 after a referendum. It reshaped how the country is governed, including devolution.
The part of the Constitution on leadership and integrity for public officers. It provides for an independent ethics commission to monitor integrity in government.

manas.q: What does Chapter Six of the Constitution cover?

children.note: Hospitals, parastatals and county bodies use public money, so they face extra rules on integrity, procurement and reporting.
Members or donors are the "owners". A SACCO board answers to members at the annual general meeting, much like a company board answers to shareholders.
Real collapses show what happens when boards, auditors and ethics fail.
A US energy company that filed for bankruptcy on 2 December 2001 after internal fraud came to light. It was then the largest US corporate bankruptcy.

manas.q: What was the Enron scandal?

children.note: Executives used accounting loopholes, misused mark-to-market accounting and used special purpose entities to hide billions in debt.
The CFO and other executives misled the board and its audit committee. The auditor, Arthur Andersen, was pressured to ignore problems and later dissolved.
The share price fell from a high of about US$90.75 to under US$1 by late November 2001.
A US law passed on 30 July 2002 after Enron and WorldCom. It set rules for public company boards, managers and audit firms.

manas.q: What law did the USA pass after Enron?

children.note: A UK report by a committee chaired by Sir Adrian Cadbury, on how boards and accounting systems should be set up. Many later codes drew on it.

manas.q: What was the Cadbury Report?

children.note: Fancy profits mean nothing without honest numbers, strong independent directors and a truly independent auditor.
Simple Kenyan cases. Read the facts, then the answer.
A hospital needs drugs. Director Wanjiru owns a pharmacy firm that quotes KES 1,200,000. Another supplier quotes KES 1,050,000 for the same drugs.
Wanjiru's private business stands to gain from the board's decision, so she has a conflict of interest.
If the board picked her firm it would pay KES 1,200,000 − 1,050,000 = KES 150,000 more for the same drugs.
Wanjiru declares her interest, it goes in the minutes, she leaves the room and does not vote. The board picks the best value quote.
A SACCO holds members' savings of KES 50,000,000. The board approves a KES 3,000,000 loan to its own chair with no security.
KES 3,000,000 ÷ 50,000,000 = 6% of all members' savings rides on one insider loan.
The chair benefits from the board's own decision. Members (the owners) were not protected: weak fairness and accountability.
Same loan rules as any member, proper security, chair absent from the vote, and the loan reported to members at the AGM.
A listed company board has 9 members: 3 executive and 6 non-executive. Of the 6 NEDs, 4 are independent.
NEDs = 6 ÷ 9 = two-thirds of the board. Independent = 4 ÷ 9 ≈ 44%. The 2 other NEDs are not independent.
A majority of NEDs gives good challenge. The audit committee should be drawn mainly from the 4 independent NEDs.
A CEO's bonus is 5% of profit. Profit is KES 20,000,000, so the bonus is KES 1,000,000. Booking KES 2,000,000 of next year's sales early lifts profit to KES 22,000,000.
New bonus = 5% × 22,000,000 = KES 1,100,000, so the CEO gains KES 100,000 from wrong early booking.
Pay linked only to short-term profit tempts managers to bend numbers. The remuneration committee should mix in long-term targets.
Small mix-ups that cost marks.
Every independent director is a NED, but not every NED is independent (e.g. a big shareholder's nominee).

children.topic: Internal audit is not the external auditor
children.note: Internal audit works inside and reports to the audit committee; the external auditor is independent and reports to shareholders.

children.topic: Chair and CEO are different jobs
children.note: Do not write that the chair runs the business. The chair leads the board; the CEO leads management.
A conflicted director must also stay out of the discussion and vote, not just mention the interest.
Lists of stakeholders should include staff, customers, lenders, suppliers, community and government.
Try each question, then open the answer steps.
Short-answer question, about 4 marks.
Define it: managers (agents) run the firm for owners (principals) but may act for themselves.
Give the cause: separation of ownership and control plus an information gap.
Give a fix: independent NEDs, audits, and pay linked to long-term results.
State the purpose of each, about 4 marks.
Audit (reporting and controls), nomination (new directors), remuneration (pay), risk (main risks). One mark each with purpose.
Name and explain four, about 8 marks.
Accountability, transparency, fairness, responsibility. For each, give a one-line meaning and a simple example.
Short videos to see the ideas explained.
A short clear intro from the Governance Institute of Australia.
A Kenyan CPA lesson on corporate governance principles for this paper.
A business professor explains principals, agents and real-world cases.
Explains the two kinds of directors and their roles.
Short lesson on audit, nomination and remuneration committees.
How Enron hid debt and why it collapsed, in about 7 minutes.
Free pages to go deeper.
Overview of how companies are directed and controlled.
More on the agency problem and agency costs.
The full story of the Enron collapse.
Background on the 2010 Constitution, including the integrity chapter.

nodeData.note: How buyers and sellers together set prices, how strongly they react to changes (elasticity), and what happens when governments fix prices. The base for pricing and revenue decisions.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Prices in a market are set by two groups: buyers (demand) and sellers (supply). Knowing how they meet helps a business set prices and forecast sales.
Any place or system where buyers and sellers trade, such as Gikomba market, an M-Pesa till or an online shop.

manas.q: What is a market in economics?

children.note: A rising price tells sellers to make more and buyers to cut back. A falling price does the opposite.
Latin for "other things staying the same". We change one thing at a time, such as price, and hold everything else fixed.

manas.q: What does ceteris paribus mean?

children.note: Budgets, sales forecasts, pricing decisions and revenue targets all depend on how customers react to price.
This is topic 1 of the paper. Later topics on costs, markets and the wider economy build on these ideas.
Demand is the amount of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, over a period of time.
The quantity buyers are willing AND able to buy at each possible price in a given period. Wanting without money is not demand.

manas.q: What is demand (effective demand)?

children.note: When price goes up, the quantity people buy goes down, and the reverse, with other things the same.

manas.q: State the law of demand.

children.note: A table listing prices and the quantity demanded at each one. Example: KES 10 → 800 mandazi, KES 20 → 600, KES 30 → 400.
A graph of the demand schedule. Price is on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal. It slopes down from left to right.
At a lower price buyers can afford more (income effect) and switch from other goods that are now relatively dearer (substitution effect).

manas.q: What two effects explain the downward demand curve?

children.note: Income, prices of related goods, tastes, population, expectations of future prices, and advertising.
More income usually means more demand for normal goods, but less demand for inferior goods.
Substitutes (tea vs coffee) and complements (cars and petrol) change demand when their own price changes.
A new fashion, a health scare, or fear that prices will rise next month all shift demand.
A normal good is bought more when income rises. An inferior good is bought less as people move to better options.

manas.q: What is the difference between a normal and an inferior good?

children.note: Substitutes are used instead of each other (bus or matatu). Complements are used together (phone and airtime).

manas.q: What are substitutes and complements?

children.note: Supply is the amount sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at each price, over a period of time.
The quantity producers are willing and able to sell at each possible price in a given period.

manas.q: What is supply?

children.note: When price goes up, sellers offer more, because selling becomes more profitable. When price falls, they offer less.

manas.q: State the law of supply.

children.note: A graph of price against quantity supplied. It slopes upward from left to right.
Costs of inputs, technology, weather, taxes and subsidies, number of sellers, and prices of other goods the firm could make.
Cheaper fertiliser or a better machine lets a farmer supply more at every price, so supply shifts right.
A good rainy season raises the maize harvest; a drought cuts it. This shifts supply, not demand.
A tax on a product raises sellers' costs and shifts supply left. A subsidy lowers costs and shifts it right.
The market price settles where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The market "clears" with nothing left over and no one queuing.

manas.q: What is the equilibrium price?

children.note: If price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer. Queues form and price tends to rise.

manas.q: What happens when price is below equilibrium?

children.note: If price is above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want. Unsold stock builds up and price tends to fall.

manas.q: What happens when price is above equilibrium?

children.note: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve. A change in anything else shifts the whole curve.
Only the good's own price changed. We call it a change in quantity demanded (or supplied).

manas.q: What causes a movement along a demand curve?

children.note: A non-price factor changed, such as income or costs. We call it a change in demand (or supply).

manas.q: What causes a shift of the demand curve?

children.note: Right means more is bought or sold at every price. Left means less at every price.
Demand up: price and quantity rise. Supply up: price falls, quantity rises. Supply down: price rises, quantity falls.
Example: school opening raises demand for uniforms, so their price and the number sold both go up.
Example: a drought cuts the maize harvest, so the price of unga rises and less is sold.
Elasticity measures how much quantity changes when something else, such as price or income, changes. It is always % change over % change.
PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. It is normally negative; we usually read its size and ignore the sign.

manas.q: What is the formula for price elasticity of demand?

children.note: Size above 1: elastic (buyers react a lot). Below 1: inelastic (buyers react little). Exactly 1: unit elastic.

manas.q: When is demand elastic, inelastic or unit elastic?

children.note: Many close substitutes, a big share of income, a luxury item, and a longer time to adjust all make demand more elastic.

manas.q: What factors make demand more price elastic?

children.note: Elastic: a price rise lowers revenue. Inelastic: a price rise raises revenue. Unit elastic: revenue stays the same.

manas.q: How does PED link to total revenue when price rises?

children.note: YED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. Positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods, above 1 for luxuries.

manas.q: What is income elasticity of demand and what does its sign show?

children.note: XED = % change in quantity of good A ÷ % change in price of good B. Positive for substitutes, negative for complements.

manas.q: What does the sign of cross elasticity tell you?

children.note: PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price. Supply is more elastic when firms have spare capacity, stock or time.

manas.q: What is price elasticity of supply?

children.note: Use average of old and new values as the base for each % change. It gives the same answer whether price goes up or down.

manas.q: What is the midpoint (arc) method for elasticity?

children.note: Sometimes a government sets a price by law instead of letting the market decide. This creates shortages or surpluses.
A legal top price, set below equilibrium to help buyers. It causes a shortage because buyers want more than sellers offer.

manas.q: What is a price ceiling and what does it cause?

children.note: Queues, rationing, black markets and lower quality can follow, because sellers have less reason to supply.
A legal bottom price, set above equilibrium to help sellers or workers. It causes a surplus.

manas.q: What is a price floor and what does it cause?

children.note: Unsold stock piles up, and the government may have to buy the surplus. A minimum wage is a floor in the labour market.

children.topic: When a control has no effect
children.note: A ceiling above equilibrium, or a floor below it, changes nothing, because the market price is already allowed.
Numeric examples in KES. Work through each one with a pen, then check the answer.
Demand Qd = 1,000 − 20P. Supply Qs = 200 + 20P (P in KES). Set them equal: 1,000 − 20P = 200 + 20P, so 800 = 40P.
P = KES 20. Q = 1,000 − 20×20 = 600 mandazi a day. Check supply: 200 + 20×20 = 600. Both sides agree.
Use the same market. Try a ceiling of KES 15 and a floor of KES 25.
A duka sells 500 kg of sugar a week at KES 200/kg. It raises price to KES 220 (+10%) and sales fall to 400 kg (−20%).
PED = −20% ÷ 10% = −2. Size 2 is above 1, so demand is elastic.
Before: 500 × 200 = KES 100,000. After: 400 × 220 = KES 88,000. Revenue falls by KES 12,000, as elastic demand predicts.
A shop sells 1,000 packets of unga a week at KES 150. Price rises to KES 165 (+10%) and sales fall to 950 (−5%).
PED = −5% ÷ 10% = −0.5. Size 0.5 is below 1, so demand is inelastic.
Before: 1,000 × 150 = KES 150,000. After: 950 × 165 = KES 156,750. Revenue rises by KES 6,750.
Price KES 200 → 220, quantity 500 → 400. Average price 210, average quantity 450.
A family's income rises from KES 40,000 to KES 44,000 a month, which is +10%.
Meals out rise from 20 to 25 a month (+25%). YED = 25 ÷ 10 = +2.5: a normal good and a luxury.
Purchases of a cheap brand fall from 10 to 9 a month (−10%). YED = −10 ÷ 10 = −1: an inferior good.
How the price of one good changes demand for another.
Tea leaves rise from KES 300 to KES 330 (+10%). Coffee sales rise from 400 to 420 packets (+5%). XED = +0.5: substitutes.
Petrol price rises 20% and car sales fall 6%. XED = −6 ÷ 20 = −0.3: complements.
Tomatoes rise from KES 80 to KES 100 a kg (+25%). Farmers bring 1,000 kg → 1,100 kg (+10%).
PES = 10% ÷ 25% = 0.4. Supply is inelastic: crops take time to grow, so farmers cannot respond fast.
Revenue peaks at KES 12,500 when P = KES 25. At that point demand is unit elastic: PED is exactly −1.
Small mix-ups cost marks. Watch for these.
Saying "demand rose" when only the good's own price fell. That is a rise in quantity demanded, a movement along the curve.
Elasticity is % change in QUANTITY on top and % change in the cause (price or income) below. Not the other way round.
Elasticity uses % changes, never raw changes in shillings or kilos. Convert first.

children.topic: Dropping the sign for YED and XED
children.note: You may ignore the minus sign for PED, but for YED and XED the sign is the whole answer.
A straight demand line has the same slope everywhere but different elasticity at each point.
A ceiling only bites below equilibrium; a floor only bites above it. Draw the diagram to check.
Short exam-style questions. Try each one before opening the answer steps.
Qd = 500 − 10P and Qs = 50 + 5P. Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
Bread rises from KES 60 to KES 66 and daily sales fall from 2,000 to 1,900 loaves. Find PED and the revenue change.
Before 2,000 × 60 = KES 120,000. After 1,900 × 66 = KES 125,400. Revenue rises by KES 5,400.
The government sets a maximum price of KES 25 in the Q1 market. What happens?
Qd = 500 − 250 = 250. Qs = 50 + 125 = 175. Shortage of 75 units, so expect queues or a black market.
Income rises 20% and demand for a product falls 8%. Calculate YED and name the type of good.
YED = −8 ÷ 20 = −0.4. It is negative, so the product is an inferior good.
Short videos that show the curves being drawn. Watch after reading the branches above.
Khan Academy explains why buyers take more when price falls, with a demand schedule and curve.
Khan Academy builds the upward-sloping supply curve from a seller's point of view.
Khan Academy puts demand and supply together to find the market price.
Khan Academy shows the difference between a shift and a movement along the curve.
Khan Academy introduces PED and how to calculate it with percentages.
Jacob Clifford gives a quick, lively summary of elastic and inelastic demand.
Free sources to go deeper.
A general overview of the model, its diagrams and its history.
More on PED, its formulas and what affects it.
How maximum prices work and what economists say about them.
Free lessons and practice on microeconomics topics.

nodeData.note: How a business's costs change as it makes more, how it picks the output that earns the most profit, and how the number of competitors (the market structure) shapes prices. Builds on topic 1: demand, supply and prices.

children.topic: Start here: firms, costs and markets
children.note: Topic 1 showed how buyers and sellers set prices. Now we look inside the seller: what it costs to produce, and how much power it has over price.

In the short run at least one input is fixed (for example, the size of the shop). In the long run every input can change, so the firm can move, build or expand. It is about flexibility, not a set number of months.

manas.q: What is the difference between the short run and the long run in economics?

children.note: Costing, pricing, budgeting and break-even work all use these ideas. Knowing fixed versus variable cost and marginal cost helps you advise a business owner on what to make and what to charge.
In the short run some costs stay the same whatever you produce, and others rise with output. Splitting them this way explains the shape of every cost curve.
Costs that do not change with output in the short run, such as shop rent, a security guard's salary or loan interest. You pay them even if you make nothing.

manas.q: What is a fixed cost? Give an example.

children.note: Costs that rise as you make more, such as flour, cooking gas, packaging and casual labour paid per piece. Zero output means zero variable cost.

manas.q: What is a variable cost? Give an example.

children.note: Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. At zero output, total cost equals fixed cost.
Average means cost per unit. AFC = FC ÷ Q, AVC = VC ÷ Q, and ATC (average total cost) = TC ÷ Q = AFC + AVC. AFC keeps falling as output rises because the same fixed cost is spread wider.

manas.q: How do you calculate AFC, AVC and ATC?

children.note: The extra cost of making one more unit: MC = change in TC ÷ change in Q. Fixed cost never affects MC, because it does not change.

manas.q: What is marginal cost and how is it calculated?

children.note: If you keep adding workers to a fixed workspace, at some point each extra worker adds less output than the one before. That is why marginal cost starts to rise.

manas.q: State the law of diminishing (marginal) returns.

children.note: Total product is all output. Average product = output ÷ workers. Marginal product is the extra output from one more worker. When marginal product falls, marginal cost rises.

children.topic: MC cuts average cost at its lowest
children.note: While MC is below the average, it pulls the average down; once MC is above it, it pulls the average up. So the MC curve crosses AVC and ATC at their minimum points.

manas.q: Where does the MC curve cut the ATC curve, and why?

children.note: In the long run the firm can choose its size. The question becomes: does getting bigger make each unit cheaper or dearer?
In the long run there are no fixed costs: the firm can sign a new lease, buy more machines or close a branch.
Usually drawn as a U shape. Cost per unit falls as the firm grows (economies of scale), flattens out, then rises if the firm grows too big (diseconomies of scale).
Cost advantages a firm gets from growing bigger, so the cost per unit falls as output rises. Types include technical, bulk buying, financial, managerial, marketing and risk-bearing.

manas.q: What are economies of scale?

children.note: Bigger firms can use larger, faster machines. A large bakery oven bakes far more loaves for not much more cost than a small one.
Big buyers get discounts. A supermarket chain pays less per bag of sugar than a single duka.
Large firms look safer to banks, so they borrow more easily and often at lower interest. They can also hire specialist managers.
Large firms can sell many products in many places, so a bad season in one area hurts less.
When a firm grows too big, cost per unit rises again. Causes: slow, garbled communication through many layers, hard coordination of many branches, and low staff morale.

manas.q: What are diseconomies of scale?

children.note: Savings a firm gets because its whole industry grows in one area, such as skilled workers, shared suppliers and better roads nearby. They come from outside the firm.

manas.q: What are external economies of scale?

children.note: If all inputs double and output more than doubles, that is increasing returns; exactly doubles is constant returns; less than doubles is decreasing returns.

manas.q: Distinguish increasing, constant and decreasing returns to scale.

children.note: The smallest output at which long-run average cost reaches its lowest level. Firms smaller than this struggle to compete on price.
Profit is revenue minus cost. Economists add one twist: they count the owner's opportunity cost as a cost too.
Total revenue (TR) = price × quantity. Average revenue (AR) = TR ÷ Q, which equals price. Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue from selling one more unit.

manas.q: Define total, average and marginal revenue.

children.note: The minimum profit that keeps the owner in this business, equal to what they could earn elsewhere. Economists treat it as a cost, so earning just normal profit means economic profit is zero.

manas.q: What is normal profit?

children.note: Any profit above normal profit. It attracts new firms into the market if they are free to enter.

manas.q: What is supernormal profit?

children.topic: Profit is highest where MC = MR
children.note: Keep producing while one more unit adds more to revenue than to cost (MR above MC). Stop where MC = MR, with MC rising. Beyond that point each extra unit loses money.

manas.q: State the profit-maximising rule.

children.note: In the short run, keep producing as long as price covers average variable cost. If price falls below the lowest AVC, stop: you lose only your fixed cost.

manas.q: When should a firm shut down in the short run?

children.note: Market structure means how many firms there are, how alike their products are and how easy it is to enter. It runs from many tiny firms to one giant.
Many small firms sell identical products, so no single firm can change the price.

manas.q: List the main features of perfect competition.

children.note: Many buyers and sellers, identical products, free entry and exit, and full information for everyone. Each firm is a price taker.
The firm can sell as much as it likes at the market price, so its demand curve is flat and price equals marginal revenue.
A firm can earn supernormal profit or make a loss for a while, depending on where price sits against its ATC.
Supernormal profit draws in new firms, supply rises and price falls until only normal profit is left. Losses push firms out until price recovers.
A single seller with no close substitutes, protected by barriers that keep rivals out.

manas.q: What is a monopoly?

children.note: Things that stop new firms entering: a government licence, patents, huge start-up costs, control of a key raw material, or strong brand loyalty.

manas.q: Give four barriers to entry.

children.note: The monopolist faces the whole downward-sloping demand curve. To sell more it must cut price, so MR is below price.
Because barriers keep rivals out, supernormal profit can continue into the long run.
When one firm can supply the whole market more cheaply than two could, such as piped water or power lines. Building two networks would waste money.

manas.q: What is a natural monopoly?

children.note: Charging different groups different prices for the same product, such as student fares. It needs market power, separate groups and no reselling between them.

manas.q: What conditions are needed for price discrimination?

children.note: Bad: higher prices, less output, less choice and less pressure to be efficient. Good: big profits can fund research, and economies of scale can lower costs.
Many firms sell similar but slightly different products, each with a little power over its own price.

manas.q: What are the features of monopolistic competition?

children.note: Many firms, free entry, and products made different by brand, location, quality or service. Each firm's demand curve slopes gently downward.
Hair salons, restaurants, chemists and boutiques in any Kenyan town: many choices, each a bit different. They compete on branding, location and service, not only price.
Free entry means new rivals copy any success, so in the long run firms earn only normal profit, though they keep some spare capacity.
A few large firms dominate the market, and each must watch what the others do.

manas.q: What is an oligopoly?

children.note: Each firm's best move depends on its rivals' reaction. If one cuts its price, the others may follow and nobody gains.
Rivals follow a price cut but ignore a price rise, so the demand curve has a kink at the current price. Prices tend to stay put even when costs change a little.

manas.q: Why are prices sticky in oligopoly (kinked demand theory)?

children.note: Firms may secretly agree to fix prices or share out customers, acting like one monopoly. This is illegal in Kenya and most countries. Mobile networks, cement and banking are markets with a few big players.
Number of firms: many, many, few, one. Product: identical, differentiated, either, unique. Entry: free, free, hard, blocked. Long-run profit: normal, normal, often supernormal, supernormal.
Without rules, big firms could fix prices or crush rivals. Kenya has a competition law and a regulator to protect fair markets and consumers.
To stop high prices, poor quality and lost choice that come from too much market power, and to give small firms a fair chance.
Kenya's competition and consumer protection regulator, often called CAK. It is the body that enforces Kenya's competition law.

manas.q: Which body regulates competition in Kenya?

children.note: Agreements between rivals to fix prices, rig bids or share markets are banned and can be investigated and penalised.
A big firm may hold a strong position but must not misuse it, for example by forcing unfair prices or terms on suppliers or customers.
Larger mergers and takeovers need approval first, so the regulator can block deals that would harm competition.
Accountants help clients spot when a deal needs merger approval, keep pricing decisions independent, and record any regulatory penalties properly.
Real numbers in KES. Work them through with a calculator and check each total.
Mama Wanjiru's kiosk pays KES 1,000 a day in rent (fixed). Output is in batches of chapati. Variable cost for 0 to 5 batches: 0; 600; 1,000; 1,500; 2,200; 3,200.
MC is the rise in TC each batch: 600; 400; 500; 700; 1,000. It falls at first, then rises as diminishing returns set in after batch 2.
AVC (1 to 5 batches): 600; 500; 500; 550; 640. ATC: 1,600; 1,000; 833; 800; 840. ATC is lowest at 4 batches (KES 800).
MC of batch 4 is 700, below ATC, so ATC still falls. MC of batch 5 is 1,000, above ATC, so ATC rises to 840. This matches the rule.
Total cars washed per day with 1, 2, 3 and 4 workers: 10, 24, 33, 38. Marginal product: 10, 14, 9, 5. After the second worker each extra worker adds less, because they share the same hoses and space.
The kiosk is a price taker at KES 900 a batch, so MR = 900. MC is 600, 400, 500, 700, 1,000.
Batches 1 to 4 each cost less to make than 900. Batch 5 costs 1,000, more than 900. So make 4 batches.
3 batches: 2,700 − 2,500 = 200. 5 batches: 4,500 − 4,200 = 300. Both are below 400, so 4 is best.
Now the kiosk is the only one at a remote site. To sell 1 to 5 batches it must charge 2,000; 1,800; 1,600; 1,400; 1,200. Costs are as in Example 1.
Batch 4: MR 800 is above MC 700, so make it. Batch 5: MR 400 is below MC 1,000, so stop. Output is 4 batches at KES 1,400 each.

children.topic: Example 5: shut down or keep going?
children.note: Lowest AVC is KES 500. At a price of 450 the best output still loses at least 1,100, worse than closing and losing only the 1,000 rent, so shut down. At 600, making 3 batches loses 2,500 − 1,800 = 700, better than 1,000, so keep going for now.
Otieno's shop shows accounting profit of KES 600,000 a year. He gave up a job paying KES 500,000. Economic profit = 600,000 − 500,000 = KES 100,000, a supernormal profit.
A small bakery makes 1,000 loaves for KES 40,000, so KES 40 a loaf. A bigger plant makes 10,000 loaves for KES 300,000, so KES 30 a loaf. Growing cut the cost per loaf by KES 10.
Small slips that cost marks in this topic.

children.topic: Mixing up average and marginal cost
children.note: Average cost is cost per unit of all output. Marginal cost is the cost of just the next unit. Label each column clearly.
Fixed cost does not change with output, so it never changes marginal cost. Work MC from the change in TC or VC; both give the same answer.

children.topic: Highest price instead of MC = MR
children.note: Profit is highest where MC = MR, not where price or revenue is highest. Always check profit at the next unit up and down.

children.topic: Treating normal profit as zero accounting profit
children.note: Normal profit is a positive accounting profit that just covers the owner's opportunity cost. Economic profit of zero is not a loss.

children.topic: Saying a monopoly charges any price
children.note: A monopolist still faces a demand curve. Raise the price and it sells less, so it cannot charge whatever it likes.
Try each one before opening the answer steps.
Fixed cost is KES 5,000 and variable cost is KES 15,000 at 100 units. Find TC, AFC, AVC and ATC.

children.topic: Q2: Should the firm make unit 201?
children.note: A price-taking firm sells at KES 50. TC rises from 4,000 at 200 units to 4,060 at 201 units.
MR = price = 50, below MC of 60. Unit 201 cuts profit by KES 10, so do not make it.
Distinguish the two market structures.
Monopoly: one firm, entry blocked. Monopolistic competition: many firms, entry free.
Monopoly: no close substitute and lasting supernormal profit. Monopolistic competition: similar branded products and only normal profit in the long run.

children.topic: Q4: Why are oligopoly prices stable?
children.note: Explain using the kinked demand curve.
If one firm raises price, rivals do not follow and it loses many customers. If it cuts price, rivals copy and it gains few.
Demand is kinked at the current price and MR has a gap, so small cost changes do not change the best price.

children.note: Shows why the long-run average cost curve is U-shaped.
Compares perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly with examples.
Uses MC = MR to find the monopoly output, price and profit.

maps.title: CA14 · 3. The economy: GDP, inflation, jobs

nodeData.note: How a whole country's output, prices and jobs are measured and managed. Covers GDP and its three measures, the circular flow and multiplier, inflation, unemployment, the business cycle and fiscal policy.

children.topic: What the economy topic is about
children.note: Earlier topics looked at one market at a time. This topic zooms out to the whole country: how much it produces, how fast prices rise and how many people have jobs.
Microeconomics studies single buyers, firms and markets (topics 1 and 2). Macroeconomics studies the whole economy: total output, the general price level and total employment.

manas.q: What is the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics?

children.note: Inflation changes costs, prices and asset values. Interest rates, taxes and demand all move with the economy, so budgets, forecasts and going-concern judgements depend on it.
The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) collects and publishes Kenya's official figures on output, prices and jobs.
Most governments aim for steady growth in output, low and stable inflation, high employment and a healthy balance with the rest of the world.
National income is the value of everything a country produces in a period, usually a year or a quarter. GDP is the most used measure.
The market value of all final goods and services produced inside a country's borders in a period, whoever owns the business.

manas.q: What is GDP?

children.note: GDP plus income residents earn from abroad, minus income foreigners earn here and send home. It measures what nationals produce, wherever they are.

manas.q: How is GNP found from GDP?

children.note: GNP minus depreciation (capital consumption), the wear and tear on machines and buildings used up during the year.
Count only goods sold to the final user. Counting maize, then the flour made from it, then the bread, would count the maize three times (double counting).
Nominal GDP uses this year's prices, so it rises if prices rise. Real GDP removes price changes, so it shows the true change in quantity produced.

manas.q: What is the difference between nominal and real GDP?

children.note: A price index for everything in GDP. Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ deflator × 100.

manas.q: What is the formula linking nominal GDP, real GDP and the GDP deflator?

children.note: GDP divided by the population. It gives a rough average output (income) per person and is used to compare living standards.

manas.q: What is GDP per capita?

children.note: GDP misses unpaid home work and much of the informal (jua kali) sector, ignores how income is shared, and does not count pollution or leisure.
Output, income and spending are three views of the same activity, so in theory all three give the same total.
Add the value each producer adds: its sales minus what it bought from other firms. This avoids double counting.

manas.q: What is the output (value added) method of measuring GDP?

children.note: Add all incomes earned from producing: wages, rent, interest and profits. Transfer payments like pensions are left out because nothing was produced.

manas.q: What is the income method of measuring GDP, and what is excluded?

children.note: Add spending on final output: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

manas.q: What is the expenditure formula for GDP?

children.note: Real data has gaps and errors, so statisticians add a balancing figure called the statistical discrepancy.
GDP at market prices includes indirect taxes such as VAT and excise duty. Factor cost removes these taxes and adds back subsidies.
Money goes round from firms to households as income and back to firms as spending. Leaks out and injections in decide whether the economy grows.
Households supply labour and get wages; they spend the wages buying firms' goods. Income paid out equals spending coming back.
Money that leaves the flow: savings (S), taxes (T) and imports (M).

manas.q: What are the three withdrawals from the circular flow?

children.note: Money that enters the flow: investment (I), government spending (G) and exports (X).

manas.q: What are the three injections into the circular flow?

children.note: National income is steady when injections equal withdrawals: I + G + X = S + T + M.
Marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is the share of each extra shilling spent; MPS is the share saved. In a simple model MPC + MPS = 1.

manas.q: What is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC)?

children.note: An extra injection raises income by more than itself, because each shilling spent becomes someone else's income. Multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS.

manas.q: What is the formula for the simple multiplier?

children.note: With an open economy and government, k = 1 ÷ (share saved + share taxed + share spent on imports). More leakages mean a smaller multiplier.
Inflation is a general, ongoing rise in prices, so each shilling buys less than before.
A sustained rise in the general price level, usually shown as the yearly percentage change in a price index.

manas.q: What is inflation?

children.note: Tracks the cost of a fixed basket of goods households buy (food, rent, transport, fuel). Base year = 100; KNBS publishes Kenya's CPI.

manas.q: What is the consumer price index (CPI)?

children.note: Inflation % = (CPI this period − CPI last period) ÷ CPI last period × 100.

manas.q: How is the inflation rate calculated from CPI?

children.note: Too much spending chasing too few goods: demand grows faster than the economy can produce, so prices are pulled up.

manas.q: What is demand-pull inflation?

children.note: Costs of production rise (fuel, wages, raw materials, taxes) and firms pass them on as higher prices.

manas.q: What is cost-push inflation?

children.note: When the shilling weakens or world prices rise, imports such as fuel and fertiliser cost more, which feeds local prices.
Deflation: prices falling. Disinflation: inflation slowing. Hyperinflation: extremely fast price rises. Stagflation: high inflation with weak growth and high unemployment.

manas.q: What is stagflation?

children.note: Borrowers gain because debts shrink in real terms. Savers, lenders and people on fixed incomes lose buying power.
Rising prices change what numbers in the books really mean, so accountants must read them with care.
Suppliers raise prices, staff ask for raises and price lists need updating often. Budgets based on last year's costs quickly become wrong.
Assets stay in the books at what they cost years ago, so they can be shown far below today's value.
Sales are at today's prices but cost of stock and depreciation use old, lower costs, so reported profit overstates real gain.
Cash and money owed to you lose value as prices rise. Collect debts fast and avoid holding idle cash.
IAS 29 Financial Reporting in Hyperinflationary Economies requires restating figures into current buying power when a currency's inflation is extreme.
Unemployed people are those able and willing to work, actively looking, but without a job.
Everyone of working age who is working or actively looking for work. Students and retirees not seeking work are outside it.
Unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.

manas.q: How is the unemployment rate calculated?

children.note: Short spells between jobs while people search, such as a graduate looking for a first post.

manas.q: What is frictional unemployment?

children.note: Skills no longer match the jobs on offer, for example when M-Pesa reduced demand for some counter clerks.

manas.q: What is structural unemployment?

children.note: Job losses when the whole economy slows and firms cut output in a recession.
Work that comes and goes with the seasons, like farm labour after harvest or tourism in the low season.
People working fewer hours than they want, or in jobs below their skills. Common in informal work.
Economies do not grow smoothly. Real GDP rises and falls around its long-run trend in repeating phases.
Output, jobs and spending grow; firms hire and invest.
Growth is at its top; the economy is close to full capacity and inflation tends to rise.
Output falls and unemployment rises. A common rule of thumb is two quarters in a row of falling real GDP.

manas.q: What is a common rule-of-thumb definition of a recession?

children.note: The lowest point before recovery starts again.

children.topic: What it means for a business
children.note: Plan for both phases: keep cash buffers in good years, watch credit risk and stock levels when sales slow.
Fiscal policy is the government using its spending and taxes to steer the economy.
Changes in government spending and taxation to influence demand, jobs and prices. Kenya's National Treasury sets this out in the yearly budget.

manas.q: What is fiscal policy?

children.note: Spend more or tax less to boost demand in a slowdown. Risk: bigger deficits and more borrowing.
Spend less or tax more to cool demand and slow inflation.
Deficit: spending is more than revenue, so the government borrows. Surplus: revenue is more than spending.

manas.q: What is a budget deficit?

children.note: Direct taxes are on income and profits (PAYE, corporation tax). Indirect taxes are on spending (VAT, excise duty).
Fiscal policy is government tax and spending. Monetary policy is the central bank (Central Bank of Kenya) managing interest rates and money supply.
All numbers below are made-up examples for practice, not real Kenyan figures.
GDP KES 12,500 bn. Income received from abroad 300, paid abroad 500, net −200. GNP = 12,500 − 200 = KES 12,300 bn.
Farmer sells maize to miller KES 20,000; miller sells flour to duka KES 35,000; duka sells it for KES 45,000. Value added 20,000 + 15,000 + 10,000 = 45,000.
Nominal GDP: year 1 KES 10,000 bn, year 2 KES 11,000 bn. Deflator year 2 = 105. Real = 11,000 ÷ 1.05 = KES 10,476 bn, so real growth about 4.8%, not 10%.
Basket costs KES 20,000 in base year, 21,500 this year, 22,575 next year. CPI 100 → 107.5 → 112.875. Inflation next year = 5.375 ÷ 107.5 = 5%.
MPC 0.8, so k = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Government spends an extra KES 2 bn on roads: income can rise by up to 2 × 5 = KES 10 bn.
Out of each extra shilling: save 0.10, tax 0.15, imports 0.15. Leakages 0.40, so k = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. KES 2 bn extra spending adds KES 5 bn.
GDP KES 12,500 bn ÷ 50 million people = KES 250,000 per person. Labour force 20 million, unemployed 1.5 million: rate 7.5%.
A pharmacy holds KES 100,000 cash for a year while prices rise 8%. It now buys only 100,000 ÷ 1.08 ≈ KES 92,593 of last year's goods.
Small slips cost easy marks in this topic.
Use net exports (X − M). Imports are spent on goods made abroad, so they are not local output.
Pensions, bursaries and gifts are not payment for production, so they are left out of GDP.
A rise in nominal GDP may be only higher prices. Always deflate before talking about growth.
Divide the change in CPI by the earlier CPI, not the later one.
If inflation drops from 8% to 5%, prices are still rising, just more slowly (disinflation).
k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). Using 1 ÷ MPC by mistake gives the wrong answer.
Try each one, then open the bubble below it to check your steps. Figures are illustrative.
C 600, I 150, G 200, X 120, M 170. Calculate GDP.
Nominal GDP is KES 1,320 bn and the GDP deflator is 110. Find real GDP.
MPC is 0.75. Investment rises by KES 5 bn. By how much can national income rise?
k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 4. Rise in income = 5 × 4 = KES 20 bn.
CPI rose from 125 to 135 over the year. What was the inflation rate?
