maps.title: CA14 · 4. Money, banks and the Central Bank of Kenya

nodeData.topic: Money, banks and the Central Bank of Kenya
nodeData.note: What money does, how banks create credit, how the Central Bank of Kenya steers interest rates and money supply, plus mobile money, SACCOs and exchange rates. Builds on demand and supply, markets, and GDP and inflation.

children.topic: What money is and why it matters
children.note: Money is anything people generally accept as payment. It makes trade easy, lets businesses keep accounts and lets the government run the economy.
Before money, people swapped goods, like a goat for maize. Barter is slow because both sides must want what the other has.
Barter only works if I want what you have AND you want what I have at the same time. Money removes this problem.

manas.q: What is the "double coincidence of wants"?

children.note: Kenya uses notes and coins (cash), bank deposits and mobile money balances such as M-Pesa. Most money today is bank deposits, not cash.
Interest rates, loan availability and exchange rates all come from this topic. They affect a firm's borrowing costs, cash flow and the cost of imported stock.
Money does four jobs and works best when it has certain qualities. Exams often ask you to list and explain both.
Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Money is accepted in payment for goods and services, so a duka owner sells sugar for shillings instead of swapping it.

manas.q: What does "medium of exchange" mean?

children.note: Money gives every item a price in one common unit, e.g. KES. This lets us compare values and keep accounts.

manas.q: What is the "unit of account" function of money?

children.note: Money can be saved today and spent later. High inflation weakens this job because money buys less over time.

manas.q: What is the "store of value" function of money?

children.note: Money is used to settle debts in future, e.g. a loan repaid in KES over 12 months.

manas.q: What is the "standard of deferred payment"?

children.note: Good money is generally acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, uniform (homogeneous), hard to forge, and limited in supply (scarce).

manas.q: List the qualities of good money.

children.note: People must trust and accept it. Its supply must be limited, or it loses value.
It should not wear out quickly and should be easy to carry. Coins and M-Pesa score well here.
It splits into small units (KES 1, 5, 10…) and every unit of the same value is identical.
It should be easy to recognise and hard to copy. Notes carry security features for this reason.
Assets easily turned into cash, like savings deposits and Treasury bills. They store value but are not spent directly.
Demand for money means how much wealth people want to hold as cash or current deposits instead of interest-earning assets. Keynes called this liquidity preference.
The wish to hold wealth in cash form, because cash is the most liquid asset. Holding it means giving up interest.

manas.q: What is liquidity preference?

children.note: People hold money for everyday spending: rent, fare, salaries. It rises with income.

manas.q: What is the transactions motive for holding money?

children.note: People hold money for emergencies, like a hospital bill or a broken-down matatu. It also rises with income.

manas.q: What is the precautionary motive for holding money?

children.note: People hold money to buy bonds or shares when prices look good later. It falls when interest rates are high.

manas.q: What is the speculative motive, and how does it relate to interest rates?

children.topic: Interest rate is the price of money
children.note: Keynes said the interest rate is set where the demand for money meets the supply of money. Higher rates make holding cash more costly.
The total money in the economy: currency held by the public plus bank deposits. Measures go from narrow (M0, M1) to broad (M2, M3).
Commercial banks take deposits and give loans. By lending most of what they receive, the banking system as a whole creates new deposits (credit).
Accept deposits, give loans and overdrafts, run payments, exchange foreign currency, give guarantees and advice.
Deposits are the bank's liabilities (it owes customers). Loans and reserves are its assets.
The part of deposits a bank keeps as cash or at the central bank instead of lending out.

manas.q: What is the reserve ratio?

children.note: When a loan is spent, it is deposited in another bank, which lends part of it again. Each round creates new deposits.

manas.q: What is credit creation?

children.note: Money multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio. Total deposits = first deposit × multiplier.

manas.q: What is the formula for the money multiplier?

children.note: Leakages cut the multiplier: people keeping cash, banks keeping extra reserves, few good borrowers, and CBK rules.

manas.q: What limits a bank's ability to create credit?

children.note: CBK is Kenya's central bank, set up in 1966 after the East African Currency Board ended. It is based in Nairobi.
The top bank of a country. It manages the currency and money supply, and it watches over other banks.
CBK's main job is to keep inflation low and stable. It also supports a stable financial system.
The key jobs a central bank like CBK does in Kenya.
Only CBK can issue Kenyan currency.
Holds government accounts, manages its borrowing (Treasury bills and bonds) and advises it.
Holds banks' reserves, settles payments between them and lends to them when short of cash.
Lends to a sound bank that runs short of cash, to stop panic spreading.

manas.q: What does "lender of last resort" mean?

children.note: Licenses and inspects banks and other deposit-takers to protect depositors.
Holds Kenya's reserves of foreign currency and gold, and watches the exchange rate.
Controls money supply and interest rates to meet its inflation goal.
The CBK committee that meets regularly to set the Central Bank Rate and announce its policy stance.
Monetary policy is how CBK changes money supply and interest rates. Tight policy fights inflation; loose policy supports growth and jobs.
The base rate CBK sets to signal its policy. A higher CBR pushes loan rates up and slows borrowing. Check the current rate on CBK's website.

manas.q: What is the Central Bank Rate (CBR)?

children.note: The share of deposits banks must keep with CBK. A higher CRR means less to lend, so less credit. Check the current figure with CBK.

manas.q: What is the cash reserve ratio and how does raising it affect lending?

children.note: CBK buys or sells government securities. Selling takes cash out of banks; buying puts cash in.

manas.q: What are open market operations?

children.note: Discount window lending, moral suasion (persuading banks), and direct credit rules or limits.
To cool inflation: raise CBR, raise CRR, sell securities. To boost growth: do the opposite.

manas.q: How does CBK tighten monetary policy?

children.note: Higher CBR → banks raise loan rates → firms borrow and invest less → spending slows → prices rise more slowly.
Kenya leads the world in mobile money, and SACCOs give members savings and loans. Both are part of the money system.
Mobile money service launched in 2007 by Safaricom and Vodafone. Users deposit, withdraw, send and pay using a phone.

manas.q: What is M-Pesa?

children.note: Agents swap cash for e-money and back. Customers' e-money is backed by money held in bank trust accounts.
It brought millions into the financial system (financial inclusion), sped up payments and cut the cost of sending money home.
CBK oversees payment services such as mobile money under Kenya's payment systems law.
Savings and Credit Co-operative Societies: members save together and borrow from the pool at fair rates.

manas.q: What is a SACCO?

children.note: Deposit-taking SACCOs are licensed and supervised by SASRA, not CBK.
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. It decides what imports cost and what exports earn.
How many shillings buy one unit of a foreign currency, e.g. KES per US dollar.

manas.q: What is an exchange rate?

children.note: Countries make what they are best at (comparative advantage) and trade for the rest. Kenya exports tea, flowers and coffee.
More shillings are needed per dollar. Imports cost more; exports become cheaper for buyers abroad.

manas.q: What happens to imports and exports when the shilling depreciates?

children.note: Fewer shillings per dollar. Imports become cheaper; exports become dearer abroad.
A floating rate is set by supply and demand. A fixed rate is pegged by the central bank. Kenya uses a market-based (floating) rate.

manas.q: What is the difference between a floating and a fixed exchange rate?

children.note: A record of all money flows between Kenya and the rest of the world: trade in goods and services, income and capital.
Step-by-step numbers in KES. All rates used here are illustrative, not current figures.
A customer deposits KES 100,000. Illustrative reserve ratio is 10%.
Bank A keeps 10% = KES 10,000 and lends KES 90,000.
The KES 90,000 is deposited at Bank B. It keeps 9,000 and lends KES 81,000.
Bank C receives 81,000, keeps 8,100 and lends KES 72,900. The rounds keep shrinking.
Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10. Total deposits = 100,000 × 10 = KES 1,000,000. New money created = 1,000,000 − 100,000 = KES 900,000.
Deposit KES 50,000, illustrative ratio 20%. Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5. Total deposits = KES 250,000; credit created = KES 200,000.
If the ratio rises from 10% to 20%, the multiplier falls from 10 to 5. The same KES 100,000 now supports only KES 500,000 of deposits, not 1,000,000.
Illustrative rate: USD 1 = KES 130. A clinic imports a machine for USD 2,000. Cost = 2,000 × 130 = KES 260,000.
If the shilling falls to KES 140 per USD, the same machine costs 2,000 × 140 = KES 280,000, which is KES 20,000 more.
A tea exporter earns KES 520,000 at an illustrative KES 130 per USD. In dollars: 520,000 ÷ 130 = USD 4,000.

children.topic: Money is not the same as income
children.note: Income is a flow earned over time; money is a stock held at a moment.

children.topic: Multiplier uses the ratio as a decimal

children.note: Total deposits include the first deposit. Credit created = total deposits minus the first deposit.
KES per USD going UP means the shilling has weakened, not strengthened.
Deposit-taking SACCOs fall under SASRA. Do not mix the regulators.

children.topic: Never quote old rates as current
children.note: CBR, CRR and exchange rates change. In exams use the figures given; at work check CBK's latest release.

children.topic: Q2: Explain three tools of CBK
children.note: Name and explain three monetary policy tools CBK uses.
Central Bank Rate (signals rates), cash reserve ratio (limits lending), open market operations (buying or selling securities). Say how each changes money supply.

children.topic: Q3: USD 3,000 import at two rates
children.note: A duka imports goods for USD 3,000. Illustrative rate moves from KES 128 to KES 135. Find the extra cost.
405,000 − 384,000 = KES 21,000 more, because the shilling depreciated.
State and explain the three motives for holding money.
Transactions (daily spending), precautionary (emergencies), speculative (waiting to buy bonds). First two depend on income; the third on interest rates.
